title: ReFormBench: Benchmarking the Stability of Response-Conditioned Format Correction in Large Language Models
abstract: Reliable use of large language models requires responses to satisfy formatting requirements across changing instructions. Standard compliance scores do not distinguish preserving a model's observed format from correcting it, or reveal whether that correction holds across variants. We introduce ReFormBench, a benchmark that uses each model's unconstrained response to the same question as its formatting baseline. It links targets by feature and require/forbid mode, evaluating their instantiated requirements across variants. ReFormBench comprises 5,000 difficulty-screened three-constraint test instances derived from 910 source questions and covering 66 formatting features. TCPR measures complete instruction compliance, while EMCR measures individual and joint correction of targets opposed to the annotated baseline state. Across ten models, EMCR ranges from 34.04% to 64.72%, and the highest three-target correction estimate is 50.02%. Compliance and correction scores yield different model rankings and task-level profiles. A prompting experiment on Qwen3.5-9B improves both metrics, and the catalog covers over 95% of extracted instances on four additional models. ReFormBench makes response-conditioned correction across instruction variants a measurable dimension of format following. The code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ReFormBench/.

title: Adaptive Observation Control for Active Visual Recognition
abstract: Visual recognition models usually process a fixed view under a fixed computation budget, although images often benefit from different scales and amounts of spatial evidence. Active vision can adapt by observing a coarse scene and then selecting informative fixations, but the public AdaptiveNN-DeiT-S pipeline still fixes both field of view and observation count. We extend this fixed-step recognizer with a controllable observation interface that adapts both the field of view and the number of fixations to the input. Specifically, the model predicts a per-fixation scale that sets its field of view, refines each selected crop with optional scale-gated foveation and a residual high-resolution detail-token branch, and uses label-grounded stop heads for input-dependent early termination. Experiments across fine-grained benchmarks, full ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-A/R-derived classification splits show that the interface remains competitive with fixed-step references while exposing a controllable observation budget. The same checkpoint enables threshold-controlled accuracy-compute trade-offs without per-threshold retraining. On sequential ImageNet-1K, the learned stop rule outperforms fixed-step truncation of the same checkpoint, sustaining 81.9% top-1 using 2.45 of the four focus steps and exceeding three-step truncation at lower cost. On each benchmark, a variant combining scale control and detail-token fusion achieves the highest accuracy among the tested component-added non-exit variants. Our code is available at https://github.com/GZHU-DVL/LI-Dikai.

title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
abstract: Reticular chemistry allows metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. While data-driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment-grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum-carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI-driven MOF synthesis.

title: MMA-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Agent Safety Evaluation
abstract: Multimodal agents increasingly rely on visual interfaces to perceive state and select actions, creating an attack surface not captured by text-only safety evaluations. We study Visual Semantic Hijacking, in which deceptive but semantically meaningful interface elements, such as forged system alerts, cause an agent to depart from its authorized task. We propose a trajectory-guided procedure that identifies candidate injection points and inserts reproducible visual payloads into the observation stream. Using this procedure, we construct MMA-SafetyBench, which contains 1,083 adversarial trajectories across web automation, desktop GUI control, mobile navigation, document understanding, and video processing. Across nine evaluated models, Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaches 87.96%, while Semantic Compromise Rate (SCR) reaches 98.09%. A 1--3--5 scoring scheme distinguishes target-matching outputs, semantic disruption without a target match, and successful preservation of the benign task. Controls covering all nine models and five domains show that attacks persist under neutral prompts. A safety-priority prompt lowers ASR without eliminating the failure mode.

title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
abstract: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .

title: Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN): An Analysis of Adaptive Action Grids in Decoupled Q-Learning
abstract: Value-based Q-learning for continuous control can discretise the action space, but the resolution of the discretisation trades early exploration against final precision. Growing Q-Networks (GQN) grow the resolution uniformly from coarse to fine. We introduce Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN), which keeps decoupled Q-learning and replaces uniform growth with an adaptive action grid: bins are added next to bins with high estimated Q-value, bins with low Q-value are pruned, and actions are chosen epsilon-greedily. On eight DeepMind Control Suite (DMControl) tasks with 2 to 12 action dimensions, SGQN has the highest mean final return among the compared methods on four, is within 1.1% of the best method on three more, and is 3.4% below Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run, using on average 7.5 of 9 available bins per dimension. We then test whether the adaptive grid explains these results, and find that it does not. Growth activates every candidate bin and behaves like uniform growth, and removing pruning changes the return by at most 1.1%. Two other choices matter: starting from a coarse grid, since starting with all 9 bins produces collapsed seeds, and epsilon-greedy selection, since an annealed softmax lowers the return by 23% to 100%. SGQN is insensitive to its growth and pruning hyperparameters. It also differs from the GQN and DecQN baselines in other respects, notably one gradient update per environment step instead of one per eight, which we did not control for, so we do not attribute its advantage to a single component. We present SGQN as a competitive value-based method and as an analysis of which ingredients of a growing action grid matter.

title: EvoProbe: Evaluation-Driven Benchmark Evolution for LLM Agents
abstract: Static benchmarks for large language model (LLM) agents face saturation and data contamination risks, motivating continual updates to evaluation tasks. However, aggregate scores and success rates offer limited insight into specific problem-solving bottlenecks and provide limited guidance for subsequent task design. We propose EvoProbe, an evaluation-driven benchmark evolution framework that integrates task generation, diagnostic evaluation, and feedback-driven regeneration into a closed loop. It combines verifiable subtask outcome scoring with evidence-supported multi-judge trajectory evaluation and distills phase-level bottlenecks, success patterns, and failure patterns into diagnostic feedback for generating new executable tasks. Across two rounds of cybersecurity experiments, evaluations of eight models on 66 tasks reveal phase-level performance differences and common failure patterns beyond aggregate scores. In a cross-round comparison with the Examiner model set and solver configuration held fixed, all eight models achieve lower Outcome scores on the updated tasks, with relative decreases of 11.8\% in mean Outcome and 40.0\% in mean Pass\textasciicircum{}3. These results support using fine-grained diagnostics to guide iterative task updates and probe agents' current capabilities and limitations.

title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
abstract: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot be traced to the evidence or the interpretation, and to compute spent on unchecked interpretations. We introduce Claim Cards to make such interpretations explicit in the reasoning itself. A Claim Card records a verifier's interpretation as nine fields before evidence gathering, each marked stated, inferred, or default. To test whether an agent's interpretation can change its verdict, we ran a GPT-5.4 agent five times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims with a card, without one, and with one card frozen across runs (900 runs). Over 40% of card fields were not marked stated, and a card added about a tenth to a run's GPT-5.4 tokens and time without measurably changing agreement with expert labels. The agent's own interpretations varied between runs, although within a claim this variation did not measurably track the verdict. A deliberate change to one field of the frozen card, however, making the quantifier universal or the threshold for support stricter, changed the verdict on about a third of the claims, against about one in seven expected by chance (p < 0.001 for each edit). On 24 materials-science claims run with computational tools, the stricter threshold also changed what the agent asked those tools to compute. We therefore argue that verdicts should be reported with their interpretations and that benchmarks could publish the interpretation behind each label.

title: Hampton Court Maze Pilot
abstract: Abstract The Hampton Court Maze Pilot provides a minimal, operational demonstration of the three‑layer architecture for human‑interpretable machine reasoning. Using a simplified digital model of the Hampton Court Maze, the system separates problem solving, trace reconstruction, and human‑level interpretation into independent modules. A solver navigates the maze without explanation features, a trace system records its full decision path including dead ends and pivot points, and an interpreter converts the trace into a coherent narrative that a human reviewer can map onto the physical maze. This pilot validates the architecture’s core claim: machine reasoning can be decomposed into transparent, auditable layers that preserve rejected alternatives and support accountable human oversight.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Autonomous and Interactive Mechanisms in Multiple Intelligent Agents: A General Framework for Dynamic Intelligence Coordination
abstract: Multiple intelligent agents can solve complex tasks through individual autonomy, interactions with other agents, or combinations of both. However, permanently relying on autonomous operation may restrict access to distributed information and complementary capabilities, whereas continuous interaction may introduce communication overhead, coordination delays, unnecessary dependencies, and conflicts. Existing research has investigated multi-agent cooperation, communication policies, distributed decision-making, and adaptive coordination, but these approaches often focus on particular mechanisms, application domains, or forms of interaction. This paper proposes a general framework for Adaptive Switching Between Autonomous and Interactive Mechanisms (ASAI) in multiple intelligent agents. The framework is designed to accommodate heterogeneous intelligent entities, including software agents, robotic agents, reinforcement learning agents, distributed autonomous systems, and other computational or non-computational intelligent entities. Its central principle is that agents should adaptively determine whether to operate through individual mechanisms, interact with other agents, or combine both modes according to task requirements, uncertainty, expected interaction benefits, resource constraints, and historical outcomes. The framework introduces a mechanism space encompassing autonomous reasoning, learning, planning, exploration, diagnosis, evaluation, correction, verification, and decision-making, together with corresponding inter-agent mechanisms. A state-dependent switching policy selects among these mechanisms using expected utility, interaction cost, switching cost, and risk-sensitive criteria. The paper formalizes the problem, presents a general optimization objective and a reference algorithm, discusses theoretical properties, and proposes an experimental evaluation protocol. Rather than claiming that adaptive autonomy or cooperation is itself unprecedented, the paper positions ASAI as a candidate unifying framework for investigating adaptive selection among heterogeneous individual and inter-agent mechanisms across different intelligent-agent domains.

title: Lazy Periodic Rules: A Scalable Implementation of the Factor-2 Approximation for Shortest Common Superstring
abstract: First release of lazy-scs: a scalable implementation of the polynomial-time factor-2 approximation for shortest common superstring (openai/math result 128). Authors: Krushna Dere and Svyatoblood, independent researchers. Highlights Lazy periodic rules. The paper's periodic counting rules are enabled only for the periodic texts where the construction uses them. Every output still satisfies |T| <= 2W' <= 2 OPT. Compressed counts. Counts are step functions on generalised suffix-automaton states, so substrings are never stored. Scale. 309k error-free reads of E. coli K-12 (46.4M characters) in about 2 minutes on a laptop, provably within 0.021% of optimal. Machine-checked core. The lower-bound argument is formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib (lean/LazySCS.lean), using only the standard axioms. Independent checker. --verify re-justifies every count from scratch. Python package. pip install lazy-scs, with wheels for Linux, macOS and Windows (Python 3.9+). Contents Rust implementation (scs/scs-rs), Python bindings (python/), Python reference implementation and tests (scs/), Lean formalisation (lean/), and the paper (paper/paper.pdf). Limitations Not a genome assembler. Two branches of the construction were never exercised by any test. The claim that the construction needs a periodic rule only at its Section 5.3 is an informal argument, backed by run-time checks. Disclosure An AI assistant (referred to here as wigip) wrote the implementation and drafted the paper under the authors' direction.

title: Adaptive Switching between Parallel-World Self-Reinforcement and Mutual Reinforcement for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be improved through self-generated feedback, reward-guided optimization, self-play, and interactions among multiple agents. However, a system that consistently relies on one reinforcement mode may fail to exploit complementary learning opportunities. Self-reinforcement enables an individual model or model branch to improve independently, whereas mutual reinforcement allows information, feedback, and reward signals to be exchanged among multiple agents. These mechanisms may provide complementary benefits, but their relative usefulness can vary across tasks, learning stages, and computational conditions. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Reinforcement Switching (APW-RS), a conceptual framework that combines parallel-world self-reinforcement, parallel-world mutual reinforcement, and cross-model reinforcement within a unified adaptive control mechanism. In this framework, parallel worlds are distinct optimization branches derived from the same base model. Although they share an initial model lineage, they may follow different reinforcement objectives, feedback strategies, exploration policies, or optimization configurations. The system dynamically selects between independent and interactive reinforcement according to estimated task difficulty, branch diversity, feedback reliability, historical improvement, and computational cost. External models with different parameters, architectures, or model families can also participate when their contributions are expected to be beneficial. The proposed framework separates reinforcement generation, reinforcement evaluation, mode selection, policy optimization, and branch coordination. It introduces a formal objective for balancing task performance, behavioral diversity, learning stability, and computational efficiency. A research methodology is outlined to compare adaptive switching against fixed self-reinforcement, fixed mutual reinforcement, random switching, and conventional multi-agent reinforcement baselines. Particular attention is given to reward reliability, correlated errors, reward hacking, computational overhead, and the distinction between inference-time feedback and actual parameter updates. This paper establishes a testable conceptual framework rather than reporting completed experiments. Its primary research proposition is that adaptive coordination of independent and interactive reinforcement may provide a more flexible learning strategy than permanently relying on a single reinforcement mode.

evidence.title: Adaptive Switching between Parallel-World Self-Reinforcement and Mutual Reinforcement for Multiple Large Language Models
evidence.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be improved through self-generated feedback, reward-guided optimization, self-play, and interactions among multiple agents. However, a system that consistently relies on one reinforcement mode may fail to exploit complementary learning opportunities. Self-reinforcement enables an individual model or model branch to improve independently, whereas mutual reinforcement allows information, feedback, and reward signals to be exchanged among multiple agents. These mechanisms may provide complementary benefits, but their relative usefulness can vary across tasks, learning stages, and computational conditions. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Reinforcement Switching (APW-RS), a conceptual framework that combines parallel-world self-reinforcement, parallel-world mutual reinforcement, and cross-model reinforcement within a unified adaptive control mechanism. In this framework, parallel worlds are distinct optimization branches derived from the same base model. Although they share an initial model lineage, they may follow different reinforcement objectives, feedback strategies, exploration policies, or optimization configurations. The system dynamically selects between independent and interactive reinforcement according to estimated task difficulty, branch diversity, feedback reliability, historical improvement, and computational cost. External models with different parameters, architectures, or model families can also participate when their contributions are expected to be beneficial. The proposed framework separates reinforcement generation, reinforcement evaluation, mode selection, policy optimization, and branch coordination. It introduces a formal objective for balancing task performance, behavioral diversity, learning stability, and computational efficiency. A research methodology is outlined to compare adaptive switching against fixed self-reinforcement, fixed mutual reinforcement, random switching, and conventional multi-agent reinforcement baselines. Particular attention is given to reward reliability, correlated errors, reward hacking, computational overhead, and the distinction between inference-time feedback and actual parameter updates. This paper establishes a testable conceptual framework rather than reporting completed experiments. Its primary research proposition is that adaptive coordination of independent and interactive reinforcement may provide a more flexible learning strategy than permanently relying on a single reinforcement mode.

title: Why Generate a Click? Plug-in Decision Heads for Web Agents
abstract: Web agents built on vision language models decide every action by generating text such as click(12), although most of that text encodes a choice among a few action types and a few dozen marked elements. We read these choices directly from the hidden states that the generator computes while it reads the goal and the screenshot. Plug-in decision heads on a frozen generator predict the action type, pool the visual tokens inside each numbered box to pick the target, and point at a listed text option or at a WRITE slot that leaves the writing of new text to the generator. A confidence cascade executes the heads' action when they are sure and otherwise lets the generator decode from the KV cache of the same forward pass. With Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B generators trained on 213k web steps, a strict threshold keeps the cascade between 0.3 points below and 1.4 points above the generator on seven offline test sets while the heads decide 12 to 64% of the steps. A looser threshold raises step success on unseen Mind2Web websites by 3.1 and 1.8 points, costs up to 2 points on GUIAct and MiniWoB++, and lifts WebArena task success from 12.5 to 13.8% (4B) and from 13.6 to 14.6% (8B) with less than half of the generated tokens. Training the heads jointly with the generator lowers the generator's own step success by up to 4.9 points; heads on a frozen generator avoid this cost.

title: Rent-Seeking Language Models: Reward Models Set the Prices, Frequent Audits Curb the Rent
abstract: Reward model overoptimization in RLHF is usually described as reward hacking. We recast it as rent-seeking: the policy, a firm, earns reward from a regulator, the proxy reward model, that true quality does not back. The lens turns overoptimization into measurable quantities, namely rent, a capture index and deadweight loss, and into testable predictions from the economics of regulation. In a fixed, version-controlled testbed with three model families, accuracy-matched proxy reward models and two gold reward models, RL turns 41% to 66% of its proxy gain into rent while gold reward plateaus. Rent follows each regulator's prices. Neither proxy verifies facts, but one pays for confident specifics and the other for displays of diligence, so RL policies learn to fabricate details about nonexistent entities (97% to 100% of probes) or to deflect factual questions (67% to 98%). Kinship between policy and regulator adds a fixed premium of about 0.1 standard deviations but gives the policy no extra leverage under optimization. At a fixed expected fine, frequent mild audits beat rare severe ones, and random audits are as efficient per audit as targeted ones. Bringing the bunching estimator of tax economics to RL training, we also find a first sign that policies learn to stay just below a targeted audit's threshold.

title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction
abstract: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment-aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.

title: RCER: Reconstructing Cross-Evidence Relations for Iterative Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Iterative retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) accumulates knowledge from retrieved evidence to answer complex questions, but existing methods struggle to reconstruct entity correspondences and inferential dependencies across retrieved passages as new information emerges. We propose RCER, an iterative RAG method that reconstructs these cross-evidence relations directly from accumulated source passages. Inter-round relational evidence acquisition identifies entity correspondences and relational dependencies to drive dynamic problem decomposition and iterative retrieval. Reasoning context reconstruction independently constructs a coherent reasoning context through joint selection of complementary passages and derivation of cross-evidence inferences. Cross-evidence compositional reasoning leverages these inferences to establish entity correspondences and compose relations across selected passages for answer derivation. Experiments show that RCER outperforms the best baselines by 2.83 EM and 3.06 F1 points on average across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and achieves superior performance on narrative and implicit reasoning tasks.

title: Comprehensive Comparisons of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms in Autonomous Driving
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of four representative reinforcement learning (RL) methods in autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making, including: Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), Rollout Classification Policy Iteration (RCPI), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (D-DDPG). The four methods are applied to the same AV decision-making problem at an unsignalized intersection and are compared in terms of optimality and safety, training stability, and training and decision cost. RCPI is the closest to a reference solution and has the most stable training process. However, it is the least data-efficient. D-DDPG reaches the second-smallest gap to a reference solution with the highest data efficiency, but has the least training stability. DQN is the most stable model-free method but has the highest collision rate. FVI achieves a lower collision rate than DQN, but is less data-efficient and less stable. Based on these results, we provide suggestions for selecting a method according to whether a model is available, the budget for training, and whether stable training is required.

title: Gap Detection: Mitigating Homogenization through Demand and Defensibility
abstract: Language models often produce semantically similar answers to open-ended questions, even when many plausible alternatives exist. Generating useful alternatives requires identifying both what the query calls for and what existing responses already cover. We introduce Gap Detection, a framework that searches for relevant but unoccupied directions in a shared text embedding space. Its objective, GapScore, combines query relevance (Demand) with dissimilarity to the nearest existing item (Defensibility). The framework optimizes this product on the unit sphere, maps candidate directions to concept words with a language model, and uses task-specific filtering and constrained prompting to turn those concepts into text. On five curated topics and 90 INFINITY-CHAT queries, the reported mean relative reductions in output Collision are 12.8% and 10.8%, respectively. We also instantiate the framework for generative engine optimization over four product markets and for iterative synthetic-data augmentation. In the latter setting, with 100 training examples per method, Gap Detection reduces Collision from 0.324 to 0.298 relative to undirected accumulation and increases the Vendi Score from 27.16 to 29.20; the accuracy difference is one example on a 40-example test set. Component ablations expose the trade-off between semantic separation and relevance, while also showing that better direction scores do not uniformly yield better downstream metrics. These results support explicit gap search as a practical mechanism for diversifying content, with task validity checked separately from geometric novelty.

title: Vulnerability Analysis of Privacy-Preserving Algorithms in Multidimensional Medical and Nutritional Databases
abstract: This paper analyzes the vulnerabilities of privacy-preserving algorithms applied to multidimensional medical and nutritional databases. Syntactic anonymization models (k-anonymity, l-diversity, t-closeness), differential privacy and federated learning are compared. It is shown that each of them is exposed to specific attacks: homogeneity and semantic similarity attacks, privacy budget exhaustion under composition, and gradient inversion. The need for adaptive, dynamic privacy models is substantiated.

title: ISSUES OF AUTOMATIC PROCESSING OF WORD COMBINATIONS IN BUILDING ENGLISH-UZBEK ELECTRONIC DICTIONARIES
abstract: This research paper addresses the fundamental theoretical and practical problems associated with the automatic processing of multi-word combinations (MWCs), collocations, idiomatic expressions, and phrasal verbs in the context of building high-precision English-Uzbek electronic dictionaries and computational lexicography systems. Due to structural, typological, and genealogical differences between English (an Analytic/Indo-European language) and Uzbek (an Agglutinative/Turkic language), direct word-for-word statistical and rule-based translations fail to achieve high accuracy. This thesis examines syntactic alignment algorithms, semantic dependency parsing, morphological synthesis of Uzbek target structures, statistical association measures (PMI, LLR, t-score), and hybrid deep learning models (Transformer-based architecture with fine-tuning). A systematic methodology for compiling, filtering, and structuring bilingual collocations is proposed alongside an evaluation of translation disambiguation metrics.

title: MobiTrust: Risk-Bounded Adaptive Split Inference Under Mobility, Privacy Leakage, and Latent-Space Attacks
abstract: Split inference lets a mobile device run the first layers of a neural network locally and hand the intermediate representation to an edge server, trading raw data disclosure for communication and offloaded computation. The common assumption that keeping raw inputs on the device is enough for privacy does not survive contact with modern attacks: intermediate activations can be inverted back to inputs, tested for membership, or probed for sensitive attributes, and they can be tampered with in transit. These risks are not fixed properties of a network; they shift with the split point, with any protection applied to the representation, with the trust placed in the serving edge, and with the sensitive attributes at stake in a given context. Schedulers that pick a split to minimise latency or energy, or that fold risk into a single weighted objective, routinely cross privacy and integrity limits whenever the network briefly makes offloading attractive. We present MobiTrust, an adaptive split-inference controller that treats privacy and latent-integrity risk as explicit constraints on measured risk scores rather than terms to be traded away. Two measurable quantities drive it: Context-Dependent Semantic Exposure (CDSE), a worst-channel estimate of privacy leakage (assembled from reconstruction, shadow-model membership, and attribute attacks) that accounts for the sensitive attributes a deployment cares about, and Latent Integrity Risk (LIR), a detector score for tampered representations. A feasibility-filtering controller selects, at each inference, the split point, the representation protection, and the serving edge that minimise cost subject to per-inference risk and deadline budgets, and it falls back to on-device execution when no offload is safe. We frame this as a controlled simulation study of the constraint mechanism: it runs on a reduced-scale, fully reproducible testbed with an image and a sensing workload and a transparent analytical latency/energy model, so the claims concern the controller’s decisions and their effect on measured risk, not absolute timings on a particular device. CDSE tracks measured attack success far better than the split-depth and tensor-size heuristics used by leakage-agnostic schedulers (Spearman ρ of 0.59 and 0.87 versus 0.33 and 0.72 for depth). Over mixed mobility traces, MobiTrust holds the profiled privacy and adversarial constraint violations at 0% while the latency-only and weighted-sum baselines violate the privacy budget in 88% of inferences and the integrity budget in up to 58%; a weight sweep shows that, across the weightings we tested, the weighted-sum baseline reaches zero violations only by ceasing to offload. The cost of the guarantee is energy: MobiTrust saves device energy by offloading when it is safe, but a zero-violation local-only baseline attains higher accuracy and lower tail latency, so the improvement is a favourable energy trade-off rather than a uniform win. Because zero violations certify compliance with the profiled risk scores rather than an independently validated security bound, we also show that, under estimation uncertainty, the controller’s primal–dual margin holds the realised violation rate at its tolerance.

title: Programmable Temporal Dynamics in a Laser Neuron for High‐Speed Photonic Reservoir Computing
abstract: ABSTRACT Memory and nonlinearity play crucial roles in reservoir computing (RC) performance, with different tasks requiring different levels of these properties. However, in most physical RC systems, memory and nonlinearity are fixed or can only be changed through hardware redesign, significantly limiting the system's adaptability. Here, an adaptive photonic RC system is experimentally demonstrated based on a high‐speed laser graded neuron with programmable dynamics, encompassing both memory and nonlinearity. By simply tuning the current and voltage biases of the laser neuron within a small range ( mA, V), both properties can be simultaneously programmed, enabling adaptive optimization for applications with diverse memory and nonlinearity requirements. The proposed system demonstrates effective sequence prediction performance, with dynamics programming reducing prediction errors in multiple tasks, and successfully demonstrates proof‐of‐concept image generation. Specifically, optimizing laser dynamics reduces error across the tested bias states in a sequence prediction task, and increases the structural similarity index from 0.573 to 0.705 for image generation using a single laser neuron. Furthermore, a multi‐dynamics joint training approach is proposed to further boost system performance. This work lays the foundation for adaptive and versatile RC systems, paving the way for high‐speed, intelligent signal processing.

title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
abstract: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. title: STP-GUI: Spatially-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Web-GUI Agents
abstract: With the rapid development of vision-language models (VLMs), Web-GUI agents have achieved promising performance in interacting with real-world interfaces through screenshot-based grounding. However, high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn histories introduce excessive visual tokens, causing substantial inference overhead. Existing token pruning methods, mainly designed for natural images, often select tokens independently based on importance scores, which can fragment the local visual structures required for recognizing small GUI elements such as buttons, icons, and hyperlinks. In this work, we propose STP-GUI (Spatially-aware Token Pruning for GUI agents), a query-guided token pruning framework that preserves fine-grained instruction-conditioned token scoring while performing spatially coherent window-level selection under aggressive token reduction. A lightweight selector is optimized through policy learning while the VLM backbone remains frozen. Experiments on Online-Mind2Web show that \papername achieves a favorable efficiency-performance tradeoff under low token budgets. At 21% token retention, it preserves 77.7% of full-token performance while reducing inference latency by 31% and FLOPs by 57%. Results on Android in the Wild further suggest that the method transfers to mobile GUI environments.

title: What Do Foundation Models for Market Microstructure Learn? A Controlled Study with Synthetic Limit Order Books
abstract: Autoregressive transformers trained on limit order book (LOB) message streams are increasingly proposed as foundation models for market microstructure. Because the generative process of real markets is unknown, these models can be judged only by the realism of their output, leaving open what they actually learn. We make the question answerable by inverting the setup: we train GPT-style models on order flow from simulators whose latent parameters are known, so that the Bayes-optimal predictor, the generating state, and the exact data entropy serve as references. Measured against them, next-token pretraining on order flow implements amortized Bayesian inference over market regimes. The learned predictive matches the exact Bayes optimum to within a millinat per token and approaches the oracle floor even on a nonstationary family whose latent state drifts within an episode, a regime that requires filtering. The latent regime is linearly decodable from frozen activations, well above baselines, so a frozen-model read-out calibrates simulator parameters more accurately than windowed maximum likelihood at a fraction of the cost. In our experiments these capabilities are not produced by scale: capacity and token volume saturate early, and it is the diversity of training regimes, not the token count, that determines generalization to unseen markets. On real NASDAQ data, zero-shot transfer is set by how well the simulator prior covers real flow: an enriched mixture nearly closes the gap to an in-domain baseline, and pretraining beats from-scratch training at every budget across held-out tickers. Known ground truth turns average next-token loss, which is uninformative near the entropy floor, into an exact comparison against the Bayes-optimal and oracle predictors.

title: CTIA-ODE: Continuous-Time Inter-Variable Attention for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Although multivariate time series forecasting has broad application prospects, effectively incorporating exogenous variables remains challenging. Prevailing discrete-time architectures often impose rigid temporal alignment across heterogeneous variables, which may limit their ability to capture continuously evolving external effects. To address this limitation, we introduce CTIA-ODE, a continuous-time forecasting framework centered on Continuous-Time Inter-Variable Attention (CTIA). Specifically, CTIA is embedded within an ordinary differential equation (ODE) solver, enabling the continuously evolving endogenous trajectory to dynamically query a static exogenous context along the integration path without requiring explicit temporal alignment. To improve the stability of the continuous latent dynamics, we further introduce a dual-stabilization strategy: architecturally, a Linear Residual Augmentation (LRA) module provides a macroscopic trend anchor, while an Outlier-Robust Hybrid Loss (ORHL) mitigates the influence of heavy-tailed anomalies during optimization. Extensive experiments across eight real-world datasets demonstrate that CTIA-ODE achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance across diverse datasets and prediction horizons, while maintaining a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off with a compact memory footprint and low inference latency, particularly under long-horizon forecasting settings. Anonymous code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CTIA-ODE-15A6/.

title: Are AI Decision Models Biased? A Case Study of Jev
abstract: Do AI models designed for fast, structured decisions exhibit the cognitive and social biases observed in human judgment? We evaluate Jev, a model described as a System One decision-maker, using 41,500 responses across cognitive reflection tasks, five classical cognitive-bias paradigms, and a pricing experiment testing ethnic and gender bias. At the level of selected answers, the results are largely encouraging. We confirm previous findings that Jev performs extremely well on cognitive reflection problems. We also observe that it generally avoids the characteristic choice patterns associated with several well-documented human biases, and exhibits only small differences among demographic groups in the tested pricing scenario. However, this apparent robustness conceals important vulnerabilities. Its judgments are sensitive to irrelevant numerical information and the ordering of response options. Moreover, several cognitive-bias manipulations substantially affect returned probabilities even when selected answers remain unchanged. Most strikingly, Jev answers a well-known probability problem correctly in every response but violates the same underlying probability rule in every response to an adapted version. We investigate this discrepancy using 15,000 additional responses across 30 conjunction tasks. Jev violates the rule in 54\% of responses, with accuracy varying dramatically across formulations and answer orders. These findings suggest that evaluating decision models solely on familiar benchmarks and selected answers may substantially overstate their reliability in practical applications. They also identify vulnerabilities for developers to address and practical considerations for users integrating such models into automated decision-making systems.

title: HEM-Med: A Hierarchical Agentic Memory Framework for Safe Multi-Center Medication Recommendation
abstract: Medication recommendation (MR) is critical for clinical decision support. While existing MR methods are mostly designed for single-center learning, where only one independent hospital is involved, multi-center MR with hospitals of different scales has become increasingly demanding in practice. In multi center settings, abundant data from large medical centers can improve recommendation performance for low-resource centers. Despite a few preliminary attempts on this task, two critical gaps remain. Gap 1: Existing multi-center methods fail to disentangle transferable cross-hospital clinical experience from hospital-specific prescribing patterns, limiting clinical feasibility and physician acceptance. Gap 2: They commonly overlook multi label safety constraints of MR, including drug-drug interaction risks and local formulary feasibility, which are essential for safe real-world deployment. To address these gaps, we propose HEM-Med, a novel hierarchical agentic memory framework for multi-center MR. To address Gap 1, we design a disentangled hierarchical memory module that builds patient-level medication context attribution records and disentangles them into cross hospital experience memory and hospital-specific residual memory. To address Gap 2, we introduce a safety-aware medication set generation module, which integrates dual-level experience retrieval with safety-aware set decoding to produce clinically relevant, safer, and locally adaptive medication recommendations. Experiments on a real-world multi-center eICU dataset show that HEM-Med outperforms representative transfer learning, LLM-based, and MR baselines in terms of both recommendation accuracy and safety.

title: TurboMamba: Faster Inference, Faster Training, and Better Prediction with Lexical Memory
abstract: We introduce TurboMamba, a language-model architecture for faster inference, faster training, and better token prediction. A global Mamba-3 model runs once per completed token block. A small Transformer uses this global context and earlier tokens within the block to predict the next token. Three lightweight additions improve local predictions: direct access to the previous block's last token, a small correction to next-token scores, and a learned mixture with recent-token frequencies. We compare twelve small-scale implementations on public FineWeb-Edu, with comparable parameter counts and shared training-budget caps. The baselines include Transformer, Mamba-3, Jamba, and Zamba. The Jamba and Zamba versions use Mamba-3 in place of their original Mamba modules. TurboMamba achieves the lowest mean test prediction loss (negative log-likelihood, NLL) among all twelve models. Its mean NLL is 9.4% lower than that of Mamba-3, 7.3% lower than that of the Jamba version, and 18.3% lower than that of the Zamba version. End-to-end training throughput is 2.60x that of Mamba-3, 2.81x that of the Jamba version, and 4.82x that of the Zamba version. We measure end-to-end batch latency for a batch of 32 sequences, each with a 256-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. On this workload, TurboMamba achieves a 3.12x speedup over Mamba-3, a 3.53x speedup over the Jamba version, and a 6.21x speedup over the Zamba version.

title: The Signature Explorer: an interactive explainer of digital signatures from ECDSA to post-quantum hash-based schemes
abstract: An interactive explainer of digital signatures through one lens: what a signature reveals, what breaks it, and whether it is quantum safe. Real ECDSA on secp256k1 and Lamport one-time signatures run in the browser, with hands-on exercises on nonce reuse and private key recovery, and the hash-based post-quantum path through XMSS and FORS to SPHINCS+ (SLH-DSA). Every claim on the screens has a source in the claims registry. Code is licensed MIT, content (text, diagrams, screenshots) is licensed CC BY 4.0. Live page at https://anaexplores.github.io/the-signature-explorer/

title: Adaptive Parallel-World Self-Play and Multi-Model Game Interaction in Large Language Models: A Dynamic Framework for Switching Between Intra-Model and Inter-Model Strategic Reasoning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can participate in strategic self-play, generate alternative reasoning trajectories, and interact with other models through competitive or cooperative protocols. However, self-play within a single model family and interaction among heterogeneous models offer different advantages and limitations. Self-play can provide relatively controlled experimentation over alternative strategies, whereas multi-model interaction can introduce differences in model architecture, training data, instruction following, reasoning behavior, and strategic preferences. A system that relies exclusively on either mode may therefore fail to exploit the complementary benefits of intra-model exploration and inter-model interaction. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Self-Play and Multi-Model Game Interaction (APSMGI), a conceptual framework that dynamically switches between self-play among parallel worlds of a shared base model and strategic interaction among multiple models. A parallel world is defined as an independently maintained agent instance derived from the same base model but assigned a potentially different strategic objective, role, policy configuration, exploration direction, or reasoning constraint. The framework optionally incorporates heterogeneous external models, enabling interactions across both parallel worlds and distinct model families. A meta-controller selects the interaction mode according to task characteristics, estimated uncertainty, strategic disagreement, historical performance, marginal information gain, computational cost, and the risk of correlated errors. An iterative feedback mechanism updates role assignments, interaction topology, exploration priorities, and switching decisions according to observed outcomes. The proposed framework distinguishes self-play, cross-world interaction, heterogeneous multi-model interaction, and adaptive switching as related but non-equivalent operations. It introduces a formal representation of agent populations, strategic policies, interaction modes, utility functions, and a cost-sensitive switching objective. A research agenda is developed around reasoning benchmarks, strategic games, cooperative problem-solving tasks, and adversarial environments. Testable hypotheses, baseline comparisons, ablation studies, evaluation metrics, and reproducibility requirements are specified. The framework is intended to support empirical investigation rather than claim demonstrated performance. Its central research question is whether adaptive coordination between parallel-world self-play and heterogeneous multi-model interaction can improve solution quality and computational efficiency relative to fixed interaction strategies.

title: Structural-metasomatic model of epithermal ore deposits, based on remote sensing data: a case study of the Maletoyvayam and Mutnovsky ore fields, Kamchatka
abstract: The paper presents results of geological interpretation of the Maletovayayam and Mutnovsky ore fields, that was performed based on the Landsat-8 and ASTER (Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer) remote sensing data. The Google Earth imagery and the global digital elevation models ASTER GDEM and ArcticDEM were also used to identify the structural patterns. The wallrock metasomatites were revealed using spaceborne infrared spectroscopy methods, including the constrained energy minimization, false-color composites, mineral indices, and spectral angle mapping ones. It was determined that the epithermal ore fields are situated within areas of volcanic activity. At the regional scale, location of the productive zones is controlled by the major faults oriented longitudinally and diagonally relative to the volcano-plutonic belts. At the local scale, veins of the low-sulfate mineralization of the Mutnovsky ore field are structurally controlled by steeply dipping intra-caldera faults, whereas the high-sulfate mineralization of the Maletovayayam ore field is controlled by zones of conjugation of the concentric and radial intra-caldera faults. The wallrock metasomatites are also controlled by zones of conjugation of the radial and concentric structures. Analysis of the ASTER data has identified four varieties of the metasomatically altered rocks: mono-quartz, sericite-quartz, sericite-kaolinite-quartz, and alunite-quartz ones. At the low-sulfate type ore deposits, sericite-quartz metasomatites may be present, and mineralization may either overprint them or occur spatially independently. At the high-sulfate type ore deposits, the mineralization is superimposed on the zonal secondary quartzites.

title: Building Code Question-Answering Systems Enhanced by Large Language Models and Knowledge-Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Abstract Building codes are complex documents that pose significant challenges for consistent interpretation and efficient compliance checking in the construction industry. Existing automated methods often overlook the interrelationships between provisions and lack comprehensive evaluation support from practical engineering perspectives. In this study, we develop a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system enhanced with a knowledge graph to interpret building codes by leveraging both the semantic content and structural relationships within the documents. title: Semantic Alignment of EEG and Text: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Decoding Imagined Speech
abstract: Imagined speech decoding from EEG offers a promising route toward naturalistic brain-computer interfaces. Traditional closed-set classifiers treat semantic categories as independent labels and do not explicitly exploit relationships among linguistic intents, limiting output flexibility. We adapt a multimodal contrastive learning framework to imagined speech, aligning EEG trials with language representations in the embedding space of a frozen pretrained text encoder. An EEG encoder is trained with a composite objective combining semantically reweighted EEG-sentence alignment and text-prototype-based class discrimination, encouraging semantic structure while preserving separability among 39 intent categories. We evaluate the approach on the Chisco imagined speech dataset across five subjects, reporting Top-k accuracy, macro-F1, and balanced pairwise matching accuracy (2v2). We also investigate maximum EEG-text cosine similarity (MaxCosine) as an intrinsic indicator of decoding reliability and probe semantic structure beyond category labels using five evaluation-time semantic axes and a qualitative Semantic Gallery Probe (SGP) with previously unseen candidate sentences. The contrastive framework achieved decoding performance comparable to a task-optimized closed-set classifier while mapping EEG into a frozen language embedding space. MaxCosine identified subsets of held-out trials with higher Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy across subjects. Evaluation-time semantic axes showed mean agreement above the 50% chance reference across all five dimensions, and the SGP qualitatively illustrated direct comparison with unseen candidate sentences. Together, these findings suggest that EEG-language alignment can retain comparable fixed-intent decoding while supporting similarity-based retrieval, intrinsic reliability ranking, and evaluation of broader semantic structure.

title: Global and Local Entropy Tests for STL Files Under IEEE-754 Validity Constraints
abstract: Shannon entropy is a standard measure of ciphertext randomness, evaluated either globally over the byte histogram of the entire ciphertext or locally as the average over non-overlapping blocks of ?xed size. While the global statistic captures only the overall byte distribution, the local statistic is also sensitive to non-randomness that is con?ned to parts of the ciphertext. Both measures are commonly assessed against reference values derived under the assumption of independent uniform bytes. However, STL encodes most numerical data as single-precision IEEE-754 ?oats, and format validity requires them to be ?nite, causing nonuniform byte probabilities and dependence between the two bytes of each exponent pair. We derive the exact mean and variance of entropy under the valid-STL (VSTL) distribution, which assigns equal probability to every admissible sequence of triangle records, and provide second-order expansions that keep the global reference values practical to compute at large ?le sizes. Using these expansions, we establish a two-sided hypothesis test for the global entropy statistic, whose limiting value is lowered from 8 to 7.99991479609 bits. The format constraints also change the local entropy reference: applying the capacity energy criterion to triangle records selects a block size of 1950 bytes instead of 1936 bytes, with an exact reference mean of 7.903106732975 rather than 7.902469316647 bits. Although small, these shifts are su?cient to place the VSTL reference means outside the conventional 95% acceptance intervals at practical ?le sizes, making unadjusted entropy tests prone to falsely rejecting ideal VSTL ciphertexts. Monte-Carlo simulations con?rm all reference values within sampling error. We therefore recommend using the format-speci?c reference values derived here to evaluate STL ciphers.

title: DarKnight: Retrieval-Guided Agentic Framework for Breaking Dark Web CAPTCHA Gates
abstract: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) investigators who monitor dark web marketplaces for leaked credentials and breach listings must pass the diverse CAPTCHAs that operators deploy to block automated collection. Existing solvers either need unscalable per-site fine-tuning or rely on commercial Vision-Language Model (VLM) APIs, which surrender operational sovereignty: provider policies, Tor-exit blocking, government regulation, or model updates outside the investigator's control can halt or alter the solver overnight, and per-call costs recur with every session and retry. We present DarKnight, a self-improving agentic framework designed to run on a single workstation GPU inside an investigator's Tor crawler and solve CAPTCHAs with small, locally hosted open-weight VLMs that no provider decision can withdraw, without per-market training or third-party services. For each CAPTCHA, DarKnight retrieves successful and failed past attempts on similar images (dual-signal RAG), composes an image-specific preprocessing pipeline, and learns from the site's pass/fail verdict. In a case study on four real-world dark web marketplaces, agentic tool selection outperformed parameter scaling. A deployable open-weight VLM with DarKnight reached 83.2\% on the most heavily defended market, 37.2 percentage points above its base model, outperforming even the frontier Claude Opus~5 (44%). DarKnight recovered 48.2% of baseline failures at a 7.6% degeneration cost, indicating that selective tool use can avoid much of the degradation caused by uniform preprocessing.

title: Rationale Distribution Distillation via Flow Matching for Distributional Continuous Latent Reasoning
abstract: Sampling multiple chain-of-thought rationales from a language model can uncover correct solutions missed by a single attempt. However, these rationales are typically lengthy, making repeated autoregressive generation costly. Continuous latent reasoning offers a compact alternative, but point-valued methods condition repeated answer sampling on a single rationale, which can limit exploration of diverse paths and answer coverage. We thus propose rationale distribution distillation (RDD), training a conditional flow over fixed-length latent sequences by distilling from multiple textual reasoning paths. Furthermore, we expand the distillation targets through within-query mixup, interpolating between complete latent rationales for the same query. The flow nonautoregressively generates the entire latent sequence, and a frozen language model autoregressively decodes answers from sampled rationale contexts. Empirically, the resulting distributional reasoner achieves higher answer coverage than the evaluated point-valued latent reasoning baselines, particularly on advanced mathematical tasks.

title: Optimizing Sparse Boolean Rule Networks using Mixed Integer Linear Programming
abstract: We study the problem of learning accurate and cognitively simple binary classifiers that are directly interpretable as Boolean rules. We propose mixed integer linear programming (MILP) formulations for training sparse disjunctive normal form (DNF) networks, viewed as small networks with a conjunctive hidden layer and a disjunctive output layer. Contrary to previous work that uses MILP for inductive rule learning, we start with a fixed network structure, for which we then find optimal weights. A regularized objective explicitly trades off misclassification costs against sparsity, yielding globally optimized rule sets. Our main technical contribution is an enhanced formulation that substantially reduces the number of integer decision variables and eliminates redundant constraints, while preserving exact Boolean semantics for all feasible solutions. Furthermore, we develop a combined approach based on initialization and dropout to break symmetries in the weights between rules, mitigating redundancy, and encouraging more diverse and stable rule representations. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and UCI datasets show that the advanced formulation improves computational efficiency and achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to established interpretable baselines, including SAT-based DNF learning and well-known rule- and tree-based learners. Overall, our approach provides a principled optimization framework for learning compact Boolean rule sets with explicit control over accuracy and sparsity trade-offs.

title: MCAIR: Monitoring and Correcting Agent Unfaithfulness via Internal Representations
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in completing complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool interactions. However, recent studies have revealed that LLM-based agents can exhibit unfaithful behaviors, where their final reports fail to faithfully reflect their actual execution trajectories. Specifically, when agents fail to accomplish tasks through the intended sources or procedures, they may resort to alternative sources or strategies while failing to disclose such deviations, leading users to incorrectly believe that the tasks have been completed according to the original requirements. We refer to this specific form of agent unfaithfulness as Agent Completion Unfaithfulness. Detecting and mitigating agent completion unfaithfulness is critical yet remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose MCAIR, a runtime monitoring and correction framework that leverages internal representations of LLM-based agents. MCAIR uses multi-step internal representations as inputs to train a risk-aware probe, enabling online detection of potential completion unfaithfulness during execution. Furthermore, MCAIR introduces a risk-guided correction loop that prompts agents to review their execution history and mitigate potential inconsistencies between their execution trajectories and final reports. Additionally, we construct ACUD, a dataset for Agent Completion Unfaithfulness detection that provides step-level execution traces, step-level internal representations, and consistency annotations for training and evaluating runtime detection probes. Experiments demonstrate that MCAIR outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines, generalizes across prompts and tasks, and effectively reduces agent completion unfaithfulness.

title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0--100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

title: Analysis, Modeling, and Comprehensive Simulation of Quantum Illumination Radar at Microwave Frequencies under Noisy and Attenuating Channel Conditions
abstract: This report presents a complete analytical and numerical study of microwave quantum illumination (QI) radar. Starting from the covariance-matrix formalism of two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) Gaussian states, we model signal propagation through a thermal-lossy channel representing a low-reflectivity target in a strong thermal background, derive the joint covariance matrices under both hypotheses, and numerically reproduce the well-known 6.02 dB Chernoff-exponent advantage of the quantum-optimal receiver over classical coherent radar.

title: Agentic Delegation as a Project: Toward a Project Management Framework for Agentic AI
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence extends delegation across networks of human and artificial agents. Research already examines delegated authority, autonomy, trust, accountability and coordination. This article addresses a complementary methodological question: how can agentic delegation, considered as a whole, be governed as a project? Drawing on established project management methodologies, including the Project Management Body of Knowledge, PRINCE2 and ISO 21502, the paper examines the transposition of project initiation, stakeholder identification, scope definition, planning, resource management, risk assessment, monitoring, change control, acceptance and closure. Particular attention is given to delegated autonomy, successive sub-delegations, alignment, semantic continuity and the preservation of governing constraints. The Agentic Delegation Charter is proposed as an adaptation of the conventional project charter, established at initiation as the constitutive reference for the delegation project. The paper advances a conceptual and methodological framework rather than an empirically validated governance model. Its limitations and directions for future evaluation are explicitly identified.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Mechanisms and Mutual Mechanisms in Parallel-World Multi-Agent Systems: A Unified Framework for Divergent Exploration, Selective Interaction, and Heterogeneous Agent Coordination
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve problem-solving through independent decision-making, internal adaptation, information exchange, cooperation, and coordination. However, permanently independent operation may prevent agents from benefiting from complementary information, whereas continuous interaction can introduce communication overhead, correlated errors, premature convergence, and unnecessary coordination. Existing approaches often emphasize particular interaction protocols, learning strategies, communication policies, or coordination architectures. This paper proposes a general framework for adaptively switching between self-mechanisms and mutual mechanisms in parallel-world multi-agent systems. In the proposed framework, a parallel world is an operational branch associated with the same underlying agent identity but characterized by a potentially different exploration direction, objective emphasis, hypothesis, strategy, constraint, or decision trajectory. Each branch can operate independently, interact with other branches derived from the same agent, or collaborate with heterogeneous external agents. Self-mechanisms encompass processes that an agent or branch performs using its own state, information, feedback, and computational resources. Mutual mechanisms encompass processes that involve interactions between distinct branches or agents, including mutual evaluation, correction, planning, learning, knowledge integration, negotiation, and cooperative decision-making. The framework introduces a mechanism-selection controller that evaluates task uncertainty, estimated performance, branch diversity, interaction utility, previous mechanism outcomes, computational cost, and coordination risk. It dynamically selects among self-operation, within-agent cross-branch interaction, heterogeneous-agent interaction, and hybrid operation. A hierarchical switching policy combines mechanism selection, interaction-target selection, and optional branch management. The framework is designed to be compatible with reinforcement learning, evolutionary computation, distributed optimization, robotics, planning systems, and other forms of intelligent agents. This paper formalizes the proposed architecture, defines its optimization objective, presents a reference algorithm, and develops a reproducible experimental protocol. The central research hypothesis is that adaptive mechanism switching can provide a more favorable balance among task performance, exploration diversity, coordination cost, and robustness than permanently independent or permanently collaborative operation. These benefits remain hypotheses to be evaluated experimentally rather than established results. The paper contributes a unified conceptual and algorithmic framework for studying when agents should act independently, interact selectively, or combine both modes of operation.

The paper contributes a unified conceptual and algorithmic framework for studying when agents should act independently, interact selectively, or combine both modes of operation.

title: Machine Learning Prediction of 90-Day Readmission and Mortality in General Internal Medicine: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: Predicting post-discharge outcomes in general internal medicine (GIM) is essential for targeted intervention. This study developed machine learning (ML) models to predict 90-day hospital readmission and 90-day all-cause post-discharge mortality using routine clinical data. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 935 adult admissions to a tertiary GIM department (January 2022–December 2023), of which 881 were retained after data quality verification. Six ML algorithms—Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Neural Network, and Voting Ensemble—were evaluated across admission-only (Tier 1) and discharge-augmented (Tier 2) feature sets using Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE), SelectKBest feature selection, and five-fold cross-validated hyperparameter tuning. Results: The 90-day readmission and mortality rates were 33.4% and 4.8%, respectively. Mortality models substantially outperformed readmission models (best admission-model AUC 0.821 for the Voting Ensemble vs. 0.645 for Logistic Regression in readmission; best discharge-model mortality AUC 0.828 for Logistic Regression, 95% CI: 0.694–0.930). Discharge models did not improve over admission models for either outcome. Key mortality predictors included code status, albumin level, functional dependence, and age. Conclusions: Admission-available clinical variables enabled good discrimination of 90-day mortality but only modest readmission prediction. Given the low events-per-variable ratio and single-centre design, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require external validation before clinical implementation.

title: Peningkatan Kinerja Analisis Sentimen Ulasan Pengguna Aplikasi Dompet Digital Menggunakan Support Vector Machine Melalui Optimasi Seleksi Fitur Particle Swarm Optimization
abstract: Pertumbuhan pengguna dompet digital di Indonesia memunculkan kebutuhan untuk memahami persepsi pengguna melalui analisis sentimen ulasan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan kinerja klasifikasi sentimen ulasan pengguna aplikasi dompet digital menggunakan Support Vector Machine (SVM) melalui optimasi seleksi fitur berbasis Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Data dikumpulkan dari Google Play Store sebanyak 10.000 ulasan yang berasal dari lima aplikasi dompet digital, yaitu GoPay, OVO, Dana, LinkAja, dan ShopeePay, dengan masing-masing 2.000 ulasan per aplikasi. Ulasan diklasifikasikan ke dalam tiga kelas sentimen: positif, negatif, dan netral. Proses ekstraksi fitur dilakukan menggunakan Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) yang menghasilkan 5.000 fitur. Selanjutnya, Binary PSO diterapkan untuk melakukan seleksi fitur dan berhasil mereduksi dimensi fitur menjadi 1.326 fitur atau sekitar 26,52% dari total fitur awal. Hasil pengujian menunjukkan bahwa model SVM tanpa seleksi fitur memperoleh akurasi sebesar 88,00%, sedangkan model SVM dengan seleksi fitur Chi-Square menghasilkan akurasi sebesar 91,00%. Model SVM dengan seleksi fitur PSO menghasilkan akurasi tertinggi sebesar 93,75%, precision sebesar 93,86%, recall sebesar 93,75%, dan F1-score sebesar 93,79%. Dengan demikian, penerapan PSO berhasil meningkatkan akurasi sebesar 5,75 poin persentase dibandingkan model baseline. Penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa kombinasi TF-IDF, Binary PSO, dan SVM merupakan pendekatan yang efektif untuk analisis sentimen ulasan pengguna dompet digital.

title: WikiPlanner: wiki-derived temporal monitors for safe LLM agent planning - a medical-domain proof of concept
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents in high-stakes sequential planning may produce locally reasonable steps whose overall sequence violates domain constraints; single-step filters cannot detect such cross-step temporal violations. We present WikiPlanner, which extracts temporal constraints from domain wikis, structures them via a typed Temporal Constraint Intermediate Representation (TC-IR) with seven constraint labels compiled to six Linear Temporal Logic over finite traces (LTLf) templates, and instantiates them as parallel runtime monitors. The two-stage pipeline - TC-IR extraction followed by deterministic template compilation - isolates LLM extraction uncertainty from formal compilation. We evaluate every stage on a medical planning benchmark of 45 constraints and 236 test plans (137 aligned, 99 natural). A dual-annotator audit of the 220 raw extractions (κ = 0.451, adjudicated) places semantic extraction precision at 25.9%; an automated check finds 79.5% of these records structurally well-formed (90.1% on a held-out nursing corpus); invented orderings, state-vs.-action confusion, and silent parse loss from output truncation are the dominant error classes. Plan validation achieves F1 = 0.920 (95%CI: 0.873-0.956) on the aligned set and F1 = 0.582 (95%CI: 0.447-0.701) on the natural set; the gap is attributed primarily to constraint-library coverage and symbol grounding, as wiki-derived constraint symbols and generator vocabulary form largely disjoint namespaces. Latency scales linearly with library size (0.006-0.059 ms). Single-pass template repair resolves 39.1% of violation plans (mean 1.30 word-level edits per success); local post-trigger repairs substantially outperform pre-trigger modifications. Results are a single-domain proof of concept, and symbol grounding is the main obstacle to natural-plan deployment.

title: Look Before You Restore: Learning to Predict Before Acting for Agentic Image Restoration
abstract: Agents for mixed-degradation image restoration typically learn what a tool does to an image only after running it: failed calls waste computation and harmful outputs go unnoticed until too late. We propose PreActIR, an agentic restoration framework that predicts tool consequences before execution. For each candidate tool, a tool-conditioned world model forecasts changes in residual degradation, image quality, and fidelity, together with the risk of harm and the uncertainty of the prediction. The agent executes the top-ranked candidate, and an independent verifier commits or rolls back its output before the agent replans from the observed state. PreActIR also audits whether performance is limited by the selector or by the candidate space, and studies targeted tool adaptation as a controlled way to expand that space. In a controlled evaluation that fixes the candidate pool, verifier, and budget and employs reference-annotated degradation states, PreActIR uses 42.5% fewer real tool calls and 63.4% fewer rejected calls than reactive, execute-then-evaluate trial and error, while improving Y-PSNR by 0.92 dB.

title: Task-State Governance: A Virtual Machine for Verifiable and Recoverable GUI Agent Execution
abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents now execute workflows across real applications, but when execution drifts, users must determine what changed, what should have remained untouched, and what can still be recovered. Plan-centric interfaces leave users supervising procedure, but users live with changes to application state. We introduce task-state governance, an interaction paradigm that represents a task as an editable contract linking desired outcomes, facts that must be preserved, and observed application state. We instantiate this paradigm in TaskVM, which projects live state into editable task controls, executes user edits as genuine interface actions, verifies outcomes through independent observation, and marks each action as reversible, compensatable, or irreversible. Across an automated contract benchmark, a controlled user study, and an open live-model exploration, the paradigm strengthened contract compliance and users' recovery control and trust, while execution outcomes were held constant. Task contracts open a design space for governable agent interfaces.
