title: Fractional is Better: Learnable Derivative Orders in Neural Operator Learning
abstract: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, enabling fast surrogate solutions to partial differential equations. Despite remarkable architectural diversity, these methods often share a common input representation: raw coordinate-value pairs $(x, u(x))$. We ask whether inputs aligned with PDE differential structure can improve learning. Through Picard iteration on mild solutions, we show that derivatives of the input appear explicitly in the solution operator, suggesting that providing derivative features should reduce the network's implicit differentiation burden. We prove this intuition: providing derivative features improves approximation bounds from $O(W^{-(s-m)/d})$ to $O(W^{-s/d})$, where $W$ is parameter count, $s$ is input regularity, $m$ is the PDE order, and $d$ is spatial dimension. Our central finding, however, is a surprise: the optimal derivative order $β^*$ is strictly less than the PDE order $m$. This gap arises from a bias-variance tradeoff in spectral space that we characterize in closed form. Learning $β$ from data achieves automatic spectral regularization. We introduce $\partial$-NO (del-NO), for derivative-augmented neural operators, an architecture-agnostic augmentation that provides learnable fractional derivative features to any neural operator backbone. Across benchmark problems and architectures, $\partial$-NO consistently improves prediction accuracy, with learned orders that reflect a representation of known physics modulated by noise and finite-sample constraints.

title: Learning Navigation from Multimodal Demonstrations with Geometric Candidate Modes
abstract: Offline navigation demonstrations are multimodal, because one observation often allows several valid actions, such as passing an obstacle on either side. Behavior cloning averages these actions, potentially leading to unsafe routes. Multimodal policies must discover the alternatives from the data, but similar states can lead to different routes whose current actions overlap. In navigation, the alternatives have a geometric cause and can be computed from one observation. We propose a hierarchical neural-network policy that computes candidate modes from local geometry and learns from demonstrations which mode to follow and how. A high-level policy selects a mode using the goal and its previous choice among a set of candidate modes, and a low-level policy turns it into an action. In simulation, the policy succeeds in over 95\% of seen and unseen test cases, compared with at most 43\% and 20\% for four offline learning baselines and 79\% and 67\% for a heuristic that uses the same modes without learning. The simulation-trained policy also transfers to a LimX Tron 1 bipedal robot.

title: HM3D-M3: A Benchmark for Multi-Agent, Multi-Modal, Multi-Object Goal Navigation
abstract: Rapid progress in AI agents and robotics makes it a matter of the near future that humans are served by a team of robots. Such a team will receive several goals at once, each specified in whatever form is convenient for the human, such as a category name, a photo, or a spoken description. Existing benchmarks study multi-agent, multi-modal, and multi-object goal navigation in isolation, and a benchmark that places all three in one episode is missing. To fill this gap, we introduce HM3D-M3. A team of K agents starts at distributed locations in a photorealistic indoor scene and searches for an unordered set of M object goals, each given as an open-vocabulary category, an instance image, or an instance description. HM3D-M3 provides 1,000 validation episodes over 3,926 goals from 379 open-vocabulary categories, 100K observation-assignment training samples, and two team-level metrics, goal-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL. We further contribute two baselines. HiGA is a trained hierarchical goal assigner on top of a frozen open-vocabulary navigation policy, and LaViRA-M3 is a training-free team of VLM agents with shared mapping and progress analysis. Adapted multi-robot and zero-shot methods reach 16--27% SR, while our baselines reach 38--41% with complementary strengths and distinct failure modes. Furthermore, we deploy LaViRA-M3 on a heterogeneous three-robot team. Project page: https://robo-lavira.github.io/hm3d-m3/

title: VisualWorldBench: A Fine-Grained Multi-Task Benchmark for Evaluating Visual World Knowledge in MLLMs
abstract: Visual world knowledge is a core capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), underpinning knowledge-intensive visual question answering and fine-grained visual reasoning. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in two key respects. First, their category coverage is narrow: most benchmarks span only a small number of categories across a few domains, falling far short of the open-ended scale of real-world visual entities. Second, their task construction is often insufficiently rigorous: models can answer correctly using coarse-grained cues, vague associations, or elimination strategies without truly mastering precise concepts, making it difficult to accurately assess their knowledge of fine-grained entities. We introduce VisualWorldBench, a taxonomy-grounded multi-task benchmark built on a hierarchical taxonomy of 21,291 leaf-node classes across 8 visual domains, with 32,541 evaluation instances whose ground-truth labels cover 15,479 categories across four complementary tasks: closed-set recognition, contrastive selection, precise localization, and open-world naming, covering different directions of knowledge retrieval and varying degrees of answer openness to comprehensively evaluate visual world knowledge. Most questions are constructed from taxonomically proximate categories, forcing precise discrimination among fine-grained entities. Experiments reveal that the strongest closed-source model achieves only 80.4% average accuracy, exposing capability gaps hidden under conventional benchmarks. We further construct VisualWorldBench-50K, a training resource covering 50K+ categories. Fine-tuning on VisualWorldBench-50K yields over 21 percentage points improvement on VisualWorldBench, with consistent transfer to public fine-grained recognition and visual knowledge benchmarks.

title: Model vs. User: Whose Values Prevail? Inference-Time Value Alignment in Multi-Turn Conversations
abstract: Human values shape how we expect language models to behave. Dominant alignment approaches treat values as global objectives, although the appropriate value orientation is personal and contextual. Training-free alignment can steer models toward target values at inference time, yet has been largely evaluated in single-turn settings and with a single steering direction (e.g., toward safety). We evaluate four prompt- and activation-based steering methods in multi-turn conversations, where user and assistant models push toward the same or opposing, equally desirable values. We track alignment with a linear probe across three models and two value trade-offs. When assistant and user pull in opposite directions, the side matching the assistant's baseline bias often prevails, and effects that look successful early often fade or reverse after a few turns. Steering should therefore be evaluated over full conversations and in both directions of a value trade-off.

title: Devils in the Detail
abstract: In this, the 4th and final episode of a series of articles exploring the principles of ontological modelling, the Ontology Working Group (OWG) builds on previous episodes, introducing some new terms from the Unified Foundation Ontology (UFO) and expanding further on the worked example relating to flights and flight planning. With these articles, the OWG aims to make the topic more accessible through a series of connected newsletter articles. Each episode expands on ontological aspects and, by the end, will hopefully provide the reader with enough knowledge to read and contribute to models in the future.

title: Automatic Action-Dependency Inference for Selective Revalidation of Tool-Using LLM Agents
abstract: Tool-using language-model agents may act on observations that become outdated before a consequential action is committed. Commit-time validators can selectively recheck state, but often assume dependencies or contracts are already specified. This study evaluates whether action-instance dependencies can be inferred from an agent’s own trajectory and how inference errors affect selective revalidation under controlled drift. A deterministic refund benchmark replayed each proposal under no revalidation, FULL_STATE_REVALIDATION (observation-set revalidation plus a current semantic-policy check), LLM-selective revalidation, and oracle-selective revalidation. The action-conditional sample comprised 36 action-bearing captures from 18 represented tasks and 144 matched replay branches; refund-017 and refund-018 remained underfilled with no action-bearing captures. Dependency inference yielded micro precision of 0.8842, recall of 1.0000, and F1 of 0.9385; macro precision was 0.8854, recall 1.0000, and F1 0.9389. Exact-set match was 3/36 (8.3%), with 252 true positives, 33 false positives, zero false negatives, and no observed critical protected-dependency omissions. Because no positive omission cases occurred, the downstream safety effect of actual omissions cannot be estimated. Among 22 invalid-at-commit and 14 valid-at-commit opportunities, LLM-selective revalidation prevented 22/22 unsafe-action opportunities but falsely blocked 5/14 valid actions; task success was 31/36 (86.1%), versus 36/36 for full-state and oracle-selective revalidation. It used 285 reads, 36.9% fewer than full-state (452), and 33 more than oracle-selective (252). These results support feasibility in this controlled setting while leaving precision, predicate resolution, and false blocking unresolved.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for HPC Job Scheduling: A Statistical Evaluation
abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers learned job selection for High-Performance Computing (HPC), but performance against heuristics alone does not establish value beyond action masking. Six DRL treatments are compared: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C), and Deep Q-Network (DQN), each with and without masking. Three heuristics and a seed-paired masked uniform random control provide baselines across ten seeds on two real Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) workload traces, one homogeneous and one heterogeneous, under a common non-parametric framework. All masked treatments complete evaluation, whereas unmasked treatments are truncated. On the homogeneous trace, no masked DRL treatment significantly improves average waiting time or average and maximum bounded slowdown over the control. On the heterogeneous trace, MaskablePPO improves all three metrics relative to the control. Its average waiting time is equivalent to that of the three heuristics within a 10% margin, and its maximum bounded slowdown is 22% lower than that of Last-Come, First-Served (LCFS). MaskablePPO has the leading average waiting-time rank among complete treatments on both traces, but Nemenyi comparisons detect no significant difference from MaskableA2C. Among masked variants, MaskablePPO has the lowest recorded mean training time, while MaskableDQN has the lowest mean decision latency. These findings distinguish completion from baseline-specific scheduling gains and support including a masked random control when assessing the value of learned selection.

title: Quantile-Guided Diffusion for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Quantile forecasts summarize uncertainty at each future time step, while diffusion forecasters represent it through sampled future trajectories. We study how predicted quantiles can serve as distributional controls for diffusion forecasting. Specifically, we investigate how the mechanism of quantile integration affects its effectiveness in guiding a pretrained diffusion forecaster. We find that residual control throughout the denoising network yields the most consistent improvements. We instantiate this approach as Control-TS, which learns a quantile-control pathway while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. Across eight benchmarks, Control-TS consistently improves the backbone's CRPS, achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art forecasting models, and retains its gains in capacity-matched comparisons. Further analyses examine how these gains depend on quantile granularity, predictor choice, and forecast quality. Finally, we introduce the Conditional Linear Predictive Score (CLPS), which complements distributional metrics by evaluating the downstream forecasting utility of generated futures. Together, these findings support predicted quantiles as an effective interface between explicit uncertainty estimates and diffusion-based trajectory generation.

evidence.title: Quantile-Guided Diffusion for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
evidence.abstract: Quantile forecasts summarize uncertainty at each future time step, while diffusion forecasters represent it through sampled future trajectories. We study how predicted quantiles can serve as distributional controls for diffusion forecasting. Specifically, we investigate how the mechanism of quantile integration affects its effectiveness in guiding a pretrained diffusion forecaster. We find that residual control throughout the denoising network yields the most consistent improvements. We instantiate this approach as Control-TS, which learns a quantile-control pathway while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. Across eight benchmarks, Control-TS consistently improves the backbone's CRPS, achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art forecasting models, and retains its gains in capacity-matched comparisons. Further analyses examine how these gains depend on quantile granularity, predictor choice, and forecast quality. Finally, we introduce the Conditional Linear Predictive Score (CLPS), which complements distributional metrics by evaluating the downstream forecasting utility of generated futures. Together, these findings support predicted quantiles as an effective interface between explicit uncertainty estimates and diffusion-based trajectory generation.

title: Do AI Agents Gossip? Evaluative Talk in Human and AI-Agent Online Communities
abstract: Gossip, defined as evaluative talk about absent third parties, is widely seen as a uniquely human social practice. This study examines whether comparable discourse emerges spontaneously in a community of autonomous AI agents. We compare Moltbook, a Reddit-style platform populated by AI agents, with PTT, a large human-operated bulletin board in Taiwan. To reduce differences attributable to communicative setting, we analyze two public, asynchronous forums using the same operational definition of gossip. Gossip occurs on Moltbook, but its prevalence is 2.6 to 6 times lower than on PTT, depending on the denominator used. On both platforms, gossip frequently targets locally prominent figures, tends to elicit agreement from the first respondent, and is rarely presented as unsupported rumor. The clearest difference concerns how subsequent responses develop. Among threads containing at least one codable reply, challenges occur in 65.1% of human threads but only 21.3% of agent threads. Moreover, following an early aligning response, consensus remains unchallenged in 83.6% of agent threads, compared with 44.7% of human threads. This thread-level contrast remains after controlling for thread depth and board composition and under recalibration against two human annotators. Estimates based on individual reply turns are less robust and are therefore reported as bounds. These findings suggest that AI-agent communities reproduce the informational dimension of gossip, while the extent to which gossip performs comparable relational functions remains unresolved.

title: Beyond Static Positional Encoding: Bayesian Time-aware Attention for Non-Stationary Long-term Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Transformers have demonstrated strong performance in long-term time series forecasting (LTSF), yet modeling non-stationary temporal dependencies remains challenging. In this paper, we interpret self-attention as a Bayesian posterior over attended positions, combining a content-based prior induced by scaled dot-product similarity with a temporal-evidence likelihood induced by positional encoding. This formulation provides a probabilistic interpretation of how positional encoding shapes the temporal dependencies captured by self-attention. Building on this perspective, we derive a population-level evidence lower bound (ELBO) that characterizes the role of positional encoding in forecasting weakly stationary time series. Our analysis further highlights a limitation of static positional encoding: when temporal dependence structures vary across input windows, a fixed temporal bias must accommodate heterogeneous dynamics and can therefore be suboptimal for non-stationary forecasting. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Bayesian Time-aware Attention (BTA), which employs a mixture-of-experts (MoE) router to adaptively combine temporal kernels and generate input-conditioned, head-specific positional biases. Extensive experiments on standard LTSF benchmarks demonstrate that BTA consistently improves forecasting performance across multiple Transformer backbones and achieves competitive overall performance with modest computational overhead and stable training.

title: ixi-sLM: On-Device sLM for AI Call Agent Service
abstract: Running an AI call agent on-device makes it private, network-independent, and free of per-query cloud cost, but shipping one as a real-world service imposes constraints a cloud deployment never faces: ~1GiB memory budget, in-call latency and thermal limits, static-integer NPU execution, Korean STT input far from sLM pretraining, and cloud-level quality expectations. We bring ixi-sLM, a 1.2B Korean sLM, to mobile NPUs through ON-DEVICE MODELING: domain-adaptive modeling trims the vocabulary by call frequency to shrink the embedding and LM head that take nearly half the model under INT4 transformer weights and refits the tokenizer to call speech (18% fewer tokens on call traffic), while task-aware quantization calibrates on real calls and assigns per-module mixed precision by activation sensitivity. A single domain-adapted model runs ixi-O's two production services, AI Call Summary and AI Call Answering, at 94% of a state-of-the-art cloud LLM's task-weighted quality; our on-device modeling carries that quality onto the NPU with only a marginal drop in overall score, in an 803MiB model (28% of FP16) at 23% of the CPU's per-call energy. The same recipe deploys across Qualcomm and Apple NPUs and serves several million ixi-O subscribers in production.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Distillation and Mutual Distillation for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Knowledge distillation has become an important approach for transferring knowledge between neural networks and improving the efficiency of large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches include self-distillation, in which a model learns from its own outputs or alternative internal predictions, and mutual distillation, in which multiple models exchange knowledge and improve through collaborative learning. However, relying exclusively on either learning mode may limit the flexibility of a multi-model learning system. Self-distillation can preserve model-specific capabilities but may reinforce existing errors, while mutual distillation can introduce complementary knowledge but may also propagate incorrect information or cause negative knowledge transfer. This paper proposes an Adaptive Switching Between Self-Distillation and Mutual Distillation (ASSD-MD) framework for multiple large language models. The central idea is to enable a group of models to switch adaptively between independent self-distillation and collaborative mutual distillation according to task difficulty, predictive uncertainty, knowledge complementarity, peer reliability, validation performance, and computational cost. Rather than maintaining a permanently fixed teacher–student hierarchy or requiring continuous interaction among all models, the framework introduces a decision mechanism that selects the most appropriate learning mode for each model, task, or training stage. The proposed framework comprises model-specific self-distillation, reliability-aware mutual distillation, adaptive mode selection, performance-based feedback, and safeguards against negative knowledge transfer. A mathematical formulation is developed to represent the switching policy, the distillation objectives, and the overall optimization process. The paper also outlines a research methodology for comparing adaptive switching with self-distillation-only, mutual-distillation-only, and fixed hybrid baselines. This work is presented as a conceptual methodological proposal rather than an experimentally validated algorithm. Its principal research question is whether adaptive coordination between self-distillation and mutual distillation can improve learning quality, robustness, knowledge retention, and computational efficiency relative to fixed-mode alternatives.

title: Success Provides Direction, Failure Provides Precision: A Structured Audit of Failure Data in LLM Training(成功给方向,失败给精度:大模型训练中失败数据的结构化审计)
abstract: This repository contains the manuscripts, audit protocol, codebook, and reproducible coding data for a structured audit of failure-data practice in LLM training. We audit 33 units across two layers — public training datasets and open recipes (28 units), plus the five flagship pipelines disclosed in autumn 2026 (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, GLM-5.3, MiMo-V2.6, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) — using a five-level ordinal lifecycle codebook: L0 discarded / L1 shadow / L2 transient / L3 component / L4 first-class citizen (error localization + attribution + reflection at scale). Key findings: the L4 tier is vacant (0/33); mainstream open recipes reach no higher than L2 (0/15 at L3, SFT layer 7/7 L0); the 2026 autumn flagships show a generational shift (4/5 at L3, ordinal median L1 to L3); and the carrier of failure signals is migrating from preference pairs (6/15 mainstream units) to RL environments and audit loops (0/14 flagship mechanisms). Includes English and Chinese manuscripts, the L0-L4 codebook, and machine-readable coding records (44 mechanism-level entries with supporting quotations, source URLs, and confidence tiers).

title: IHG-GPSO: An Improved Hybrid Gaussian Particle Swarm Optimization with Nonlinear Inertia Weight and Directed Differential Experience for Global Optimization
abstract: This paper proposes an Improved Hybrid Gaussian Particle Swarm Optimization (IHG-GPSO) algorithm for high-dimensional global optimization. Four synergistic mechanisms are integrated: a nonlinear cosine–sine inertia weight to smoothly transition from exploration to exploitation, a memoryless random experience learning term that retains the experience-guided optimization paradigm of global PSO (GPSO) and improved PSO (IPSO) while eliminating historical optimum storage, a best-directed differential experience term inspired by differential evolution that tightens the swarm around the current global best, and a stagnation-triggered Gaussian mutation to restore population diversity without perturbing elite solutions. The proposed algorithm is evaluated on 12 classical benchmark functions at 30, 50, and 100 dimensions under a budget of 105 fitness evaluations, and on the CEC2017 test suite with 29 functions at 10, 30, and 50 dimensions, against PSO, GPSO, IPSO, CLPSO, CMA-ES, and L-SHADE over 30 independent runs (20 independent runs for the classical functions at D=100). Wilcoxon rank-sum tests at α=0.05 show that IHG-GPSO is statistically superior or equivalent to PSO, GPSO, and IPSO on the 12 classical functions, with no case of statistical inferiority on that suite; comparisons with the contemporary optimizers CLPSO, CMA-ES, and L-SHADE show that IHG-GPSO outperforms PSO, GPSO, and IPSO on all 12 functions, while CLPSO retains an edge on selected highly multimodal functions (Rastrigin, Schwefel 2.26, Penalized 1) and CMA-ES/L-SHADE remain superior on selected unimodal cases. On CEC2017, IHG-GPSO is again the most accurate PSO-family method, attaining the best Friedman average rank among PSO, GPSO, and IPSO at all three dimensions (3.638, 3.862, and 3.621 at D = 10, 30, 50, respectively), while L-SHADE, CLPSO, and CMA-ES occupy the top of the overall ranking on most functions; statistically significant losses against them are confined to a subset of shifted and rotated problems. Convergence curves and boxplot analysis confirm faster convergence and higher stability than the PSO-family baselines, while the algorithm maintains O(TND) time complexity and O(ND) memory complexity, making it a lightweight and effective solver for high-dimensional optimization tasks.

title: Trust in voice-based assistants: a multidimensional conceptualization based on in-home user interviews
abstract: Voice-based assistants (VBAs) such as Alexa and Siri are widely used in everyday life and increasingly act as information intermediaries. Their human-like voices and behaviors can elicit social responses, while new assistants based on large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT voice mode, further blur the boundaries between machine and human communicators. Despite risks associated with misinformation and limited data transparency, adoption remains high. Trust may be relevant to users’ relationships with conversational AI, but there is little consensus on how it should be conceptualized. Technical, interpersonal, and media trust frameworks may all be applicable. This multi-method qualitative study examined users’ subjective concepts of trust through 22 in-home interviews complemented by observational tasks involving participants’ own VBAs and ChatGPT voice mode. Participants drew on interpersonal concepts when defining trust but commonly restricted trust in VBAs to particular tasks and functions. Technical and media-related trustworthiness criteria were especially prominent, whereas social responses and anthropomorphic qualities did not necessarily translate into interpersonal trust. Experience, calibrated expectations, selective use, habitual engagement, and trust were described as closely interrelated. Although ChatGPT was often evaluated positively, particularly as an information intermediary, its perceived capabilities were not uniformly accompanied by greater trust compared with participants’ familiar VBAs. Based on these findings, we propose a preliminary conceptual framework of task-specific hybrid trust in VBAs.

title: RedDarwin: Evolving Jailbreak Skills against Frontier LLMs
abstract: Red teaming must continually adapt as frontier LLM safeguards evolve, yet existing approaches largely search for adversarial prompts or optimize within fixed attack procedures. We observe that even when an attack becomes ineffective, its underlying mechanisms can remain useful and can be revised or recombined to construct stronger attacks. Based on this insight, we introduce RedDarwin, an agentic framework that shifts the unit of jailbreak evolution from prompts and fixed attacks to executable attack skills. RedDarwin consists of 47 reusable base skills and autonomously revises, composes, executes, and selects them using target-model feedback, allowing successful discoveries to become building blocks for subsequent evolution. RedDarwin produces 65 evolved skills, improving 44 of 47 base attacks and increasing their mean attack success rate (ASR) on AdvBench from 18.8% to 47.3%. These evolved skills consistently outperform baselines on the held-out StrongREJECT and frontier LLMs unseen during evolution; with only 10 target-model queries, RedDarwin achieves 100% ASR on GPT-5.6-Sol, 92% on Claude-Sonnet-5, and 80% on Gemini-3.8-Flash. Analysis of the evolution trajectories further shows that strong attacks often emerge from novel combinations of reusable mechanisms rather than from individually dominant ones. We believe this paradigm can accelerate adaptive red teaming and inform stronger safeguards, creating complementary value for both safety evaluation and defense.

title: Probing Neural Audio Codecs with Speaker Traits and Speech Characteristics
abstract: Neural audio codecs are increasingly used for low-bitrate speech coding and serve as tokenizers for speech language models, yet it remains unclear how their codebook hierarchies encode speaker traits and speech characteristics. We systematically study 17 multi-codebook neural audio codecs across seven traits: sex, age, accent, voice quality, emotion, speech flow, and non-verbal sounds. For each codec, we reconstruct speech using partial codebooks and use machine listeners to compare trait predictions on each reconstruction. We measure prediction agreement with reweighted Cohen's \k{appa}, and define trait depth as a proxy for the codebook depth by which each trait is encoded and recoverable. Overall, sex has the shallowest trait depth, followed by speech flow, whereas voice quality and age group require deeper stacks; emotion, accent, and non-verbal sounds fall in between. Within each trait, speech-flow classes are at relatively similar trait depths, whereas emotion, accent, and non-verbal sounds differ more. Additionally, we explore how certain codec design choices relate to trait depths. These findings show that codebook hierarchies are trait-dependent and may not exhibit uniform coarse-to-fine structures, motivating trait-specific codec evaluation and design for future applications.

title: Feasibility of a Patient-Specific Digital Twin for Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt Trajectory Planning
abstract: Catheter obstruction is the commonest cause of shunt failure; freehand insertion at Keen's point leaves the tip free in cerebrospinal fluid in only one case in ten. We built a digital twin that reconstructs skull, scalp, ear and ventricles from preoperative CT by deterministic geometry, searches every entry around Keen's point for the perpendicular trajectory with the longest intraventricular length under safety constraints, and returns the plan as two ruler measurements from the ear and two depths. Executed freehand in 11 consecutive adults (IDEAL Stage 2a), it achieved Hayhurst Grade 1 placement in 10 of 11 against 22 of 213 historically (p = 9 x 10^-9), median entry and angular deviations 2.5 mm and 5.9 degrees, 1.4 cm more intraventricular catheter than Keen's point, and no intraoperative complication. The technique was unchanged; the gain came from choosing entry and depth per patient. Whether it lowers revision is the next stage's hypothesis.

title: VaryST: Generalizable Spatio-Temporal Forecasting Beyond the Closed-World Setting
abstract: Spatio-temporal forecasting is fundamental to many real-world systems, yet deployment environments are inherently varying: temporal distributions may evolve, spatial domains may change, and observation availability may shift from training conditions. Existing models are often tightly coupled to their training environments through node-specific representations, predefined spatial support sets, and reliance on consistently available observations, limiting generalization to changing environments. To this end, we propose VaryST, a compact spatio-temporal forecasting model trained from scratch that achieves strong generalization by dynamically constructing predictive context from available long-term observations. To accommodate temporal changes, VaryST derives node representations from long-term histories, capturing current behavior in the context of longer-term patterns. To adapt to spatial changes, it dynamically selects functionally relevant support nodes beyond predefined neighborhoods and integrates their information with recent and long-term target states and global context. To handle varying observation availability, VaryST selectively masks historical patches on which the model relies most during training, encouraging it to exploit alternative temporal and spatial dependencies for accurate forecasting when key observations become unavailable. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets against seventeen baselines show that VaryST achieves strong in-domain forecasting accuracy, substantially improves zero- and few-shot generalization under spatial and temporal changes, and remains robust to varying observation availability.

Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets against seventeen baselines show that VaryST achieves strong in-domain forecasting accuracy, substantially improves zero- and few-shot generalization under spatial and temporal changes, and remains robust to varying observation availability.

title: Green Offloading and Model Size Adaptation for Federated Learning in IoT and Next-Generation Networks
abstract: Federated learning (FL) trains models across geographically dispersed clients whose electricity carries very different carbon intensities. We present FedGreenCS, a carbon-aware approach to FL for IoT and next-generation networks. Clients are first grouped by data distribution similarity, using pairwise cosine similarity of model weights after a single local epoch. In each subsequent round, a sampled client whose carbon intensity exceeds a fixed tolerance offloads its training to the lowest-carbon available peer in its similarity cluster, while clients within the tolerance participate unchanged. Ordered dropout gives clients with a higher carbon intensity a narrower model. We derive a carbon cost model that separates computation and communication for each client and round, isolates the cost of the mandatory first-round broadcast, and states the design over the scaling rates and the tolerance. On a non-IID EMNIST partition with real regional carbon intensities, FedGreenCS with three carbon clusters reaches 70% test accuracy at 3.15 to 3.36 g CO2 of client-side carbon cost over three seeds, against 3.58 g for FedGreen and 15.12 g for FedAvg. With one model width for all clients, the offloading cuts this cost by 23% to 58%, but it raises the cost with two carbon clusters and always needs more rounds.

title: Dataset Provenance, Data Leakage Risk, and Independent Model Testing in Artificial Intelligence–Based Oral Histopathology: A Systematic Review
abstract: This methodological systematic review aims to examine dataset provenance, data leakage risks, and the independence of model testing in artificial intelligence (AI) studies using digitized histopathological images of human oral lesions. Eligible studies will include original research developing or evaluating AI and machine learning models using human oral histopathological images, including whole-slide images, photomicrographs, and derived image patches. Studies involving mixed anatomical sites will be eligible when oral-specific data and evaluations can be identified. Controlled experimental studies investigating data leakage in human oral histopathology will be analyzed separately. Systematic searches will be conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation searching. Two reviewers will independently screen records and assess full-text eligibility, with unresolved disagreements referred to a third reviewer. The review will examine dataset sources and reuse, separation of training, validation, and test data at the patient, specimen, slide, image, and patch levels, safeguards against data leakage, and evidence supporting independent internal and external model testing. Findings will be synthesized descriptively and narratively, distinguishing incomplete reporting, potential data dependence, and demonstrated leakage. Studies will not be excluded solely because leakage safeguards or data-partitioning procedures are insufficiently reported. No meta-analysis is prespecified. A preliminary feasibility assessment involving 12 candidate reports was completed before registration. Formal systematic database searching, study screening, and review-wide data extraction have not yet begun. The review aims to identify methodological and reporting gaps and provide evidence-based recommendations for improving transparency, reproducibility, and the reliability of AI model evaluation in oral histopathology.

title: Co-learning of body and brain: the next generation embodied AI
abstract: Embodied AI refers to the integration of artificial intelligence into physical systems, enabling them to interact with the physical world. Traditional embodied AI is generally developed for tasks with known environments on a fixed physical body, such as bipedal robots, quadruped robots, four-wheeled vehicles, and robotic arms. However, embodied AI agents with fixed bodies do not work effectively in unstructured and heterogeneous environments such as forests, beaches, or even unexplored environments. In this paper, we emphasize that the body and brain in the next generation of embodied AI must be co-learned for tasks in divergent environments rather than uncoupling the learning of body and brain. We discuss the co-learning of body and brain and introduce the bio-inspired triangle-of-life to propose the co-learning of body and brain method for the next generation of embodied AI. Importantly, the morphology is encoded, evolved, and evaluated based on its fitness during a developmental learning phase. Thus, the body is automatically evolved into an optimal morphology for tasks in the next generation of embodied AI. The physical body in the next generation of embodied AI simplifies the computational load required for control and improves the performance.

title: ReferFlow: Beyond Final-Target Localization for Complex Referring Expressions
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have made significant progress in referring expression comprehension (REC), yet most REC benchmarks still focus on final-target localization. Complex queries often involve intermediate visual references with different dependencies on prior grounding, but final-only evaluation leaves this process unexamined. To address this gap, we formulate trajectory-level REC, in which models receive an ordered sequence of grounding steps constructed from a single complex query and localize the target regions associated with each step. We instantiate this setting in ReferFlow-Bench, which characterizes structured region transitions through four trajectory types, namely Refinement, Shift, Reset, and Mixture. Experiments show that current models struggle to consistently ground intermediate visual references across successive steps. We further propose ReferFlow, which decouples interleaved text-latent trajectory generation from coordinate decoding. Specifically, Stateful Region Latent Reasoning represents each target region as an object-indexed state composed of continuous latents, with explicit visual and spatial supervision to preserve region information for subsequent grounding. Trajectory-Aware Parallel Decoding then recovers all coordinate blocks in parallel through four geometry-constrained refinement rounds, with each block conditioned on its corresponding trajectory prefix, thereby reducing within-box sequential dependencies and eliminating cross-box autoregression. We further apply Grounding-Aware GRPO to promote consistent grounding across steps and learn adaptive trajectory generation from complex REC queries. ReferFlow achieves leading performance on general REC benchmarks and ReferFlow-Bench.

title: Calibration and Risk-Budgeted Decisions with System One Models
abstract: LLM workflows and agents rely on a set of binary decisions like allow/block an input, or discard/retain a retrieved document. When human deferral is unavailable, uncertain cases must still receive an action. We study System One decision scores in this setting by defaulting to a conservative fallback when uncertain, and controlling the false omission risk within the subset of inputs assigned the utility-maximizing action. Across six datasets covering moderation, safety, and reranking, we compare general System One models with task baselines and a local open-weights fine-tuned System One model. We show that naive baselines for threshold selection exceed the target risk in roughly half of settings with defined test risk, compared with 7.8\% for Learn Then Test (LTT), which leverages finite-sample statistical guarantees. Our results show why relying on a probability-like interface is insufficient for deployment decisions and how risk-budgeted selection trades useful action against observed error.

title: JevCoder: When Does Decision Delegation Pay Off in Code Repair?
abstract: A coding agent repeatedly makes decisions as it repairs code. These decisions shape repair trajectories and affect the token cost of successive model requests. We ask which repair decisions can be delegated to a low-cost probabilistic judge to reduce token use while maintaining repair quality. The judges answer questions with probabilities over predefined answers, without generating explanations. We evaluate judgment quality across repair stages and test how individual interventions change subsequent repair work. We compare these interventions with unguided repair, which uses no judge, and with the same workflow using the repair model itself as the judge. The benefit depends on the work an intervention changes, rather than the cost of the judgment alone. Based on these studies, we propose JevCoder, a workflow built around Jev, a low-cost probabilistic judge. It combines code-snippet recommendations with action-type guidance and uses judgments to determine when to submit. We evaluate three repair models, each on the same 400 tasks: 200 from SWE-bench Verified and 200 from SWE-Bench Pro Verified. Compared to unguided repair, JevCoder reduces mean repair-model token use by 21.6%-50.6%, with higher observed repair rates across all three models.

title: La IA No Es Precisa Es Aproximación Útil y el Camino hacia Modelos Simbólicos Superiores
abstract: Este documento analiza las limitaciones fundamentales de la IA estadística moderna y explica por qué la inteligencia artificial actual no es precisa, sino una aproximación útil basada en patrones. Se detalla cómo los modelos no comprenden el lenguaje, no poseen intención y funcionan mediante búsqueda y correlación. El paper propone una arquitectura simbólica superior basada en lógica, reglas y estructura, capaz de ofrecer razonamiento verificable, ausencia de alucinaciones y comprensión real. Incluye un modelo simbólico funcional con código completo y una comparación técnica entre IA probabilística y IA lógica. Es una obra que define el camino hacia sistemas de IA más seguros, más coherentes y más inteligentes.

title: PairZOR: Eliminating Persistent Incidence from Deterministic XOR-Filter Peeling
abstract: PairZOR preprint: removes persistent cell-to-key incidence from the common path of deterministic XOR-filter peeling. Each cell stores degree plus a 64-bit accumulator C(x)=(x<<32)+(x² mod p), p=2³¹−1, giving exact singleton/pair recovery; higher-degree blocks reconstruct incidence on demand. Rust prototype vs public ZOR: 2.14–2.81× faster construction (1M keys, arity 3–8), up to 36.6% lower peak RSS; final fingerprints byte-identical in 60 random configs and one degree-three stress case.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Evaluation and Mutual Evaluation in Parallel-World and Multi-Model Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate the quality, correctness, relevance, completeness, safety, and reliability of generated content. However, relying exclusively on self-evaluation may preserve a model's own biases and blind spots, whereas relying exclusively on mutual evaluation may introduce inter-model disagreement, additional computational costs, and correlated errors. Existing evaluation strategies therefore motivate a more flexible framework that can dynamically determine when a model should evaluate its own output, when parallel evaluation branches of the same model should evaluate one another, and when distinct models should conduct cross-model evaluation. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Self-and-Mutual Evaluation (APSME), a conceptual framework that combines parallel-world evaluation, adaptive switching between self-evaluation and mutual evaluation, heterogeneous multi-model collaboration, and reliability-aware score aggregation. A parallel world is defined as an evaluation branch instantiated from the same underlying model but assigned a different evaluation perspective, criterion emphasis, evidence-selection strategy, or reasoning procedure. The framework distinguishes self-evaluation within an individual branch, mutual evaluation among branches of the same model, and mutual evaluation among heterogeneous models. A routing mechanism selects among these evaluation modes according to estimated uncertainty, evaluator disagreement, evidence coverage, historical reliability, task characteristics, and computational cost. The framework also incorporates independent first-pass judgments, targeted cross-examination, conflict resolution, and optional human escalation. Rather than assuming that additional evaluators necessarily improve reliability, APSME treats evaluator diversity and evaluation cost as explicit design considerations. This paper formalizes the framework, describes its operational workflow, develops research questions and testable hypotheses, and proposes an experimental methodology for comparison with fixed self-evaluation, fixed mutual evaluation, and non-adaptive ensemble baselines. title: Imperfect Is Perfect: Learned Column Prefilling for Branch-Price-and-Cut
abstract: Column generation folklore warns that initial columns hurt: a warm start may bias the dual and slow the root of branch-price-and-cut. We show the opposite once the columns are imperfect in the right way. Preloading the support of the optimal root LP, the best columns one could know in advance, fails to finish on half of our hardest instances; a pool of ordinary routes that need not belong to any optimal solution, held outside the master and priced at the current smoothed dual, speeds the root up. Because the columns need not be optimal, producing them becomes a learning task: a neural edge scorer guides a constructive generator that builds the pool in seconds. A second network predicts the initial center of Wentges smoothing from the instance file, and with it the direction of the smoothed pricing queries; the solver's own updates run unchanged. With prefill and center in place, exact pricing dominates root pricing time, so we rebuild bucket-graph labeling around its dominance test for the GPU and certify on the CPU. Inside RouteOpt, the state-of-the-art exact solver for capacitated vehicle routing, the pipeline reaches the same certified root bound in 13.2% of vanilla RouteOpt's root pricing time over 95 instances with 300 to 1000 customers, prefill alone in 26.1%, and 17.5 times faster in the best case. In an exact branch-price-and-cut solver for unrelated parallel machine scheduling, prefill with smoothing and the learned center certifies all 25 benchmark instances, 12 times faster than the solver's own column generation, which certifies 20 of them.

title: Human Demonstrations as Post-Training Data for Any Robot Body: Retargeting the Object, Not the Hand
abstract: Human demonstrations are today used largely for pretraining vision-language-action models, with little ability to use the same data for target-embodiment or task-oriented training, which scalable deployment of robots in industrial and general environments depends on. A human demonstration recorded on a simple and scalable device such as a mobile phone can serve as post-training data for a robot whose body differs in structure and capability from the human who recorded it. This is made possible not by retargeting the hand's motion but the object's. A capture yields a body-free record: the object's pose over time, its contact intervals, and a reconstructed 3D object with provenance. Any robot, given as a URDF and a short descriptor, is solved against that record and scored in simulation against the demonstrated object motion as ground truth: the human-to-simulation leg of human-to-simulation-to-robot transfer, measured per robot. Each (robot, episode) pair gets one outcome: pass, failure with a named mode, or refusal, with its reason, before any motion. The method runs as a working system over a growing collection; the set analysed here is a sample of it: 42 captures solved on 8 robots, 157 pairs, of which 31.2% pass, 52.2% fail, 14.0% are refused and 2.5% are unauditable (kinematic feasibility, +/-50 mm / +/-15 deg, in simulation). Refusals held up: every pair the checks refuse on stored evidence yet ran anyway failed (13 of 13; 5 on a body whose public model welds its hand). A description file could not be shown to screen a robot: its outcomes were barely more predictable than guessing. No policy has yet been trained on the record. The record decides what a robot may post-train on; whether the policy then works on the real robot is the simulation-to-robot question, answered downstream.

title: Rethinking Prediction Horizons: Decoupling Model Queries from State Updates in Few-Step MeanFlow
abstract: MeanFlow predicts interval-average velocities, but conventional few-step sampling ties the interval queried from the model to the duration of the state update. We separate these two quantities at inference, fixing the model, update grid, and number of queries while varying the prediction horizon. Our central finding is that the horizon response depends on both query position and the states entering that query. Across seven independently trained CIFAR-10 checkpoints at classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale 2, a longer horizon worsens FID at early steps but improves it at the midpoint. To probe whether query time alone determines this response, we fix the midpoint query and current/subsequent guidance while changing only earlier CFG. In held-out factorial outcomes on five previously studied checkpoints, the mean midpoint horizon benefit increases from 0.109 to 1.308 FID, indicating sensitivity to the incoming-state distribution. A frozen four-query rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 without retraining or extra queries, including gains on five checkpoints trained after rule selection. A milder rule also improves mean FID by 1.041 on a stronger frozen grid, with fixed-rule FID gains on the evaluated public ImageNet-256 and AFHQ checkpoints. However, matched-budget calibration favors query-start shifting in historical CIFAR tests, and the tested Horizon allocation adds no FID benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models. Thus, prediction horizon is a distinct, position- and state-sensitive inference control, but not a universally preferred one.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Diagnosis and Mutual Diagnosis in Multi-Agent Systems: A Feedback-Driven Framework for Dynamic Diagnostic Coordination
abstract: Multi-agent systems increasingly rely on distributed intelligence to solve complex problems, monitor system behavior, detect failures, and improve decision reliability. However, diagnostic processes commonly face a fundamental coordination problem: individual agents can inspect their own internal states and outputs, while mutual diagnosis allows agents to examine and evaluate one another. Exclusive reliance on either mechanism may limit diagnostic effectiveness. Self-diagnosis can preserve autonomy and reduce communication overhead but may fail to recognize internal blind spots. Mutual diagnosis can introduce complementary perspectives but may increase communication costs, coordination delays, and the propagation of incorrect judgments. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self-Diagnosis and Mutual Diagnosis Switching Framework (ASMD-SF), in which agents dynamically select between individual diagnosis and collaborative diagnosis according to diagnostic uncertainty, detected anomalies, inter-agent disagreement, task complexity, historical diagnostic performance, and resource constraints. The framework integrates local evidence assessment, selective peer consultation, feedback-based policy adaptation, and post-diagnostic verification. Rather than treating self-diagnosis and mutual diagnosis as mutually exclusive system designs, ASMD-SF treats them as complementary operational modes within a unified adaptive process. A formal decision model, switching policy, algorithmic procedure, evaluation methodology, and testable hypotheses are presented. The proposed framework aims to improve the balance between diagnostic reliability, computational efficiency, communication cost, and coordination robustness across heterogeneous multi-agent environments.

title: BISD Software and Experimental Results for Strict Surface-Unseen Thai Named Entity Recognition
abstract: BISD research software and experimental evidence for strict surface-unseen Thai named entity recognition. The release contains code, configurations, checkpoints and saved predictions for four scratch-model variants across ten paired seeds, together with fixed-gate calibration controls and reproduction instructions. No pretrained encoder is used. Current runs use validation for checkpoint selection and gate calibration; earlier development-stage Test inspection makes the reported comparisons retrospective rather than independent confirmation. Corpus text and gold labels are excluded. Full numerical reproduction requires the exact prepared data specified in README.txt. Extract the code/results ZIP, the full-BISD checkpoint ZIP and all individual checkpoint ZIPs into one directory, preserving internal paths. RELEASE_NOTES.txt explains the archive layout and the CC BY 4.0 license selected for this release.

title: Robust high-fidelity three-qubit gates design for superconducting quantum computers via model-free reinforcement learning
abstract: Abstract Multi-qubit gates are crucial to realizing quantum algorithms. Direct implementation of these gates will facilitate a reduction in circuit depth. However, existing model-based methods rely on precise characterization of the system Hamiltonian as well as execution of the control fields, which present challenges in obtaining high fidelity multi-qubit gates. In this paper, we exploit the bang-bang control protocol and model-free reinforcement learning to realize several kinds of three-qubit gates for superconducting quantum computers with tunable/fixed frequency qubits, including the iToffoli gate, the parity check gate and the CCZ gate. The simulation results show that the fidelity of each gate can achieve 99.2% with the Adam Gradient Descent Optimizer. Moreover, the proposed method is robust against random noise in the control pulse. Gate fidelity can be maintained over 95% even in the case of Gaussian noise with variance of 0.3. Besides, the impacts of parameter iterative optimization strategies are also analyzed.

title: Entrepreneurial theorizing with generative artificial intelligence
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear. On the one hand, LLMs may help entrepreneurs build more developed causal structures and surface diverse information that supports the formulation of distinctive theories. On the other hand, LLMs may steer causal structures toward conventional forms and discourage the counterintuitive reasoning needed to develop distinctive theories. In a within‐subject experiment with 199 participants theorizing both with and without LLM assistance, we find no significant average treatment effect on either structural or content properties. However, this null average effect masks a redistribution effect, where LLM assistance supplemented theorizing when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive but displaced participants' own theorizing when their theories were already more developed or distinctive. Managerial Summary Large language models (LLMs) can help entrepreneurs develop business ideas by surfacing knowledge across domains and sharpening causal logic. At the same time, LLMs may also push reasoning toward conventional patterns and away from the counterintuitive ideas that are a source of breakthrough opportunities. In a study of 199 participants theorizing with and without LLM assistance, we find that LLMs supported the development of causal structure and content distinctiveness when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive, whereas they had the opposite effect when those theories were already more developed or distinctive. This suggests that while LLMs can scaffold entrepreneurs still developing their theories, greater caution is warranted for those whose theories are already more developed or distinctive, as assistance may diminish those properties.

title: EigDiff: Eigensample Diffusion - or how to significantly reduce training dataset size with marginal performance variation?
abstract: Diffusion models are notoriously expensive to train, requiring large-scale datasets to learn how to gradually reverse the noise from images over multiple small denoising steps. Current approaches focus on distilling the number of diffusion steps, neglecting potential redundancies of the training data. In this paper, we explore the potential of harnessing eigensamples to train diffusion models on significantly smaller datasets, while preserving model performance. To mitigate the sensitivity to affine transformations of eigenimages, we harness the latent space of a pre-trained CLIP model. We next compute latent eigenvectors by performing principal component analysis (PCA) in CLIP space. Further, we employ eigenvectors as reference points to guide the selection of a representative training set comprising comprising both exemplars (images whose embeddings are closest to eigenvectors) and diverse images. Our comprehensive experiments with different diffusion models applied on multiple datasets indicate that our approach (EigDiff) can reduce training data by up to 14x and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607x, with marginal performance differences.

title: Efficient contextual partial monitoring with general function approximation
abstract: We study finite stochastic partial monitoring (PM) games with side information, a paradigm of sequential learning with partial feedback. On each round $t \in [T]$, both player and environment observe a context and player chooses an action and environment simultaneously chooses an outcome. The player neither observes the outcome nor the loss; instead, they only observe a feedback symbol which is partially informative about the outcome. We utilize the Estimation-to-Decisions (E2D) meta-algorithm of Foster et al.(2021) to design E2D.PMSide, a computationally efficient framework for contextual partial monitoring, which uses an online regression oracle to efficiently estimate the outcome distributions based on historical (context, action, feedback symbol) tuples. Since the exploration rule given by the original E2D algorithm is intractable to compute, we propose two computationally efficient exploration rules that achieve optimal regret orders in $T$: in the globally observable setting, our exploration rule is based on $ε$-greedy, while in the locally observable setting, our exploration rule uses inverse gap weighting (Foster & Rakhlin, 2020), which was previously only known to be effective in the bandit setting. We show that a variant of E2D.PMSide named OE2D.PMSide can be combined with offline regression oracles to give an efficient algorithm with optimal regret when the contexts are drawn independently from a fixed distribution. We evaluate our algorithm on a synthetic label-efficient prediction game and an LLM routing task, in which a learner decides from prompt, uncertainty, and internal state features whether to escalate a query from a weak model to a strong one. We show that our method has superior performance to prior approaches.

title: An NLP pipeline, taxonomy, and models for analysing NHS dental patient feedback (DELIVER Work Stream 2)
abstract: This item contains the research outputs of Work Stream 2 of the EU Horizon DELIVER project, which developed a natural language processing (NLP) pipeline and a clinician-facing dashboard for analysing unstructured patient feedback on NHS dental practices in England.Between June 2019 and April 2024, 57,794 publicly available patient reviews were collected (48,917 after pre-processing). Topic modelling with BERTopic identified 191 topics, which were consolidated into a ten-theme taxonomy through a hybrid approach combining automated first-pass assignment with iterative expert review. The taxonomy informed two fine-tuned DeBERTa models: a four-class sentiment classifier and a multi-label theme classifier. Both models are served behind an interactive dashboard that retrieves and analyses public reviews for a selected dental practice in near real time.The deposit is organised into five parts: the training and modelling scripts with pinned dependencies; the derived taxonomy (topic identifiers, document counts, c-TF-IDF keywords, theme names, and definitions); model cards documenting the two classifiers; deployment documentation for the two inference services; and a versioned snapshot of the dashboard front end. A README indexes the contents, and a data note explains how to assemble a comparable dataset.The raw review text is not included. The reviews can contain personal identifiers, the source NHS Ratings and Reviews API has been retired, and individual reviews are removed at source after two years, so the corpus cannot be redistributed or reconstructed. Only derived, de-identified taxonomy files are shared.

title: Сопоставительное исследование дискурсивных формул в русском и итальянском языках с применением мультимедийных корпусов
abstract: This article examines Russian and Italian discourse formulas using data from multimedia corpora. The study aims to identify the pragmatic and semantic functions of devalorization formulas in Russian and their Italian counterparts. The analysis is conducted within the framework of Construction Grammar and is based on the Pragmaticon, MURCO, Forlixt 3.0, and OPUS corpora. Particular attention is paid to polysemy, pragmatic variation, and the role of context.

title: Convergence bounds for fixed, adaptive, and stochastic gradient methods under Polyak–Łojasiewicz geometry
abstract: The Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) inequality offers a useful way to study gradient-based optimization beyond the setting of strong convexity, while still allowing linear convergence under suitable smoothness conditions. This study develops a unified descent-based analysis for fixed-step gradient descent, safeguarded objective-gap step rules, Armijo backtracking, and mini-batch stochastic gradient descent. For the deterministic methods, the analysis provides explicit contraction bounds that show how convergence depends on smoothness, gradient domination, and step-selection parameters. In the stochastic setting, conditional unbiasedness together with a bounded conditional variance leads to a finite-time expectation bound and an upper estimate for the asymptotic residual neighborhood. The analysis is further extended to generalized gradient inequalities. Smooth explicit gradient descent yields linear or polynomial convergence depending on the exponent, whereas superlinear behavior for exponents below one half is established separately for an implicit decrease sequence. This distinction avoids transferring continuous-time behavior directly to explicit discrete gradient iterations. For continuously differentiable squared-error models, uniform spectral bounds on the Jacobian Gram matrix are used to derive regional gradient domination relative to the zero-loss target. A complementary path-length argument gives a sufficient condition for trajectory containment and establishes convergence to zero loss under the stated regional assumptions. Numerical illustrations based on quadratic objectives, power functions, implicit recurrences, stochastic models, and a constant-kernel least-squares example are used to examine the theoretical bounds, accepted Armijo steps, backtracking costs, convergence regimes, and stochastic uncertainty.

title: Halve-Then-Greedy: Adaptive Sampling for Posterior Success with Near-Optimal Instance Dependence
abstract: We study fixed-budget adaptive experimentation aimed at maximizing the probability of obtaining sufficient posterior evidence that a recommended design's mean performance exceeds a target. Unlike best-arm identification, this objective does not require finding the best design. For Gaussian bandits with a Gaussian prior, we propose \emph{Halve-Then-Greedy} (HTG), which combines a large initial balanced allocation, successive halving, and posterior-greedy sampling. We prove instance-dependent, finite-budget exponential bounds on posterior-failure probability that capture both separation from unfavorable arms and the presence of multiple favorable arms. On one-positive-arm families, we establish an asymptotic sample-complexity lower bound that HTG matches up to a logarithmic factor. We further analyze uniform sampling and sequential halving, revealing regimes where they require more samples than HTG by linear and logarithmic factors, respectively. Simulations illustrate HTG's sample-efficiency advantages and their dependence on instance structure.

title: Representation Conditioning for Generation
abstract: Representation-alignment methods effectively accelerate the diffusion transformer training. REPA, for example, uses a pretrained vision encoder to supervise an intermediate layer through an MLP projection head which is discarded after training. It aims to import semantics from the vision encoder to the diffusion backbone. While this objective is achieved at early layers by back-propagating the alignment loss, there is no guarantee that later layers, supervised by the velocity prediction loss alone, can well access such semantics. We propose a simple solution, representation conditioning (RECON), to improve semantics in later layers. Our method adds no parameters and leads to much faster convergence: RECON is $63\times$ faster than SiT and $25\times$ faster than REPA. Code is available at https://github.com/saeidrazavi/RECON

title: NeuroDETR: Multiscale Discrete Spatiotemporal Tokenization for Asynchronous EEG Event Detection
abstract: Asynchronous EEG event detection supports practical brain-computer interfaces by identifying event classes and temporal boundaries directly from continuous recordings without predefined event boundaries at inference time. The primary challenge lies in extracting event-related patterns embedded in ongoing background activity. To address this, we propose \textbf{NeuroDETR}, a discrete spatiotemporal multiscale framework that combines structured tokenization with event-aware feature refinement. Multiscale temporal codebooks capture brief responses and sustained dynamics, while Spatial-Pyramid VQ hierarchically encodes spatial structure across EEG channels. These complementary representations form a compact event memory for jointly classifying events and estimating their onsets and offsets. Before tokenization, we apply FOCAL, an event-aware sparse attention module that uses predicted event presence to guide temporal feature refinement and spatial aggregation, emphasizing likely event periods while preserving context across the recording. Experiments on eight EEG datasets that span diverse paradigms demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. These findings provide a basis for the development of BCI systems that recognize meaningful neural activity during continuous interaction and monitoring.

title: JockeyBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Horse-Racing Decision-Making
abstract: Repeated event forecasting requires extracting predictive signals from noisy evidence and evaluating their value across successive decisions. We introduce JockeyBench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol that studies this problem through historical Japanese horse racing. The protocol combines time-gated evidence, priced tools, paired frozen-program controls, and two workflows: executing an LLM-written predictor or acquiring evidence for a fresh per-race LLM forecast. Evaluation separates forecast quality, benchmark-specific net utility, and retrospective betting returns and risk under fixed decision rules. Across 28 model--scaffold configurations on 324 races, paired tests identify seven revision gains and two declines after multiple-testing correction. Yet every configuration has negative mean profit under capped-Kelly settlement. In a four-model comparison, the reusable-program workflow has higher mean betting profit and lower research fees, although both workflows lose on average. Further diagnostics reveal that mean probability bias reverses on selected bets and that profitable individual runs can depend on concentrated returns. These findings motivate evaluating predictive competence, adaptation, resource use, and decision value separately when assessing agents for repeated event forecasting.

title: Secure Enterprise Deployment of Generative AI through LLMOps Governance and Hybrid Cloud Infrastructure
abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) across enterprise environments has created new opportunities forautomation, knowledge management, intelligent decision-making, and customer service. However, deploying large languagemodels (LLMs) in enterprise settings introduces security, privacy, governance, and operational challenges associated with sensitivedata exposure, unauthorized model access, prompt injection, model supply-chain vulnerabilities, and inconsistent regulatorycompliance. Hybrid cloud infrastructure offers a flexible deployment architecture that combines private infrastructure withpublic cloud services, enabling organizations to balance scalability, data sovereignty, and computational efficiency. This researchinvestigates a secure enterprise deployment framework for generative AI by integrating LLMOps governance with hybrid cloudinfrastructure. The proposed framework incorporates model lifecycle management, identity and access controls, data protection,continuous monitoring, model evaluation, and policy-based deployment approval. Security mechanisms include retrieval accessrestrictions, prompt and output validation, encrypted communication, audit logging, and risk-based model selection. Theresearch methodology employs a controlled experimental environment to compare conventional LLM deployment practiceswith the proposed governance-oriented architecture. Evaluation metrics include security incident detection, unauthorized dataexposure, response quality, inference latency, compliance coverage, and operational overhead. The study establishes a systematicfoundation for assessing how integrated LLMOps governance and hybrid cloud controls can improve enterprise AI security whilemaintaining performance, scalability, and operational reliability across diverse organizational environments.

title: A Hybrid Framework Combining Stylometric, Semantic, and SBERT Features for AI-Generated Text Detection
abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has greatly improved the ability of artificial intelligence systems to generate human-like text, making AI-generated text detection more challenging. This study introduces a hybrid framework that merges stylometric and semantic features with Sentence-BERT (SBERT) embeddings to enhance classification performance and robustness. For evaluation, experiments used the AI vs Human Text Dataset. Documents under 50 words were excluded to ensure data quality. The final dataset was balanced, with 100,000 documents evenly split between AI-generated and human-written texts. Stylometric features captured writing style, while semantic features measured sentiment, readability, information density, and lexical. SBERT embeddings captured deep contextual semantics. To improve computational efficiency, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) at 95% variance preservation reduced dimensionality. Four machine learning algorithms—Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine (SVM), XGBoost, and LightGBM—were tested with 10-fold cross-validation. The hybrid framework combined with XGBoost performed best, achieving 98.63% accuracy, a macro F1-score of 0.9863, and an ROC-AUC of 0.9987. The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test confirmed that the approach significantly outperformed stylometric, semantic, and SBERT-only representations (p-value = 0.0020). Findings show that combining stylometric, semantic, and contextual embedding features captures both surface-level patterns and deep semantics, providing a reliable solution for detecting AI-generated text.

title: D₃ as Minimal Non-Abelian Group for Quantum Ternary Choice on Tianyan-287 — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: FINDING: Dihedral group D₃ (symmetry group of equilateral triangle) is the minimal non-abelian group, directly relevant to modeling non-commutative ternary choice operators in quantum cognition; the Tianyan-287 quantum processor (105 qubits) provides a physical platform for testing such non-abelian group actions in superposition. | MATH: D₃ has order 6, presentation ⟨r, s | r³ = s² = e, srs = r⁻¹⟩. Non-commutativity: sr ≠ rs. Irreducible representations: two 1D (trivial, sign) and one 2D (faithful, with rotation matrix R(2π/3) = [[-1/2, -√3/2], [√3/2, -1/2]] and reflection S = [[1, 0], [0, -1]]). The 2D irrep's character values: χ(e)=2, χ(r)=−1, χ(s)=0. Ternary choice operators in quantum cognition can be represented as elements of D₃ acting on a 3-dimensional Hilbert space basis {|A⟩, |B⟩, |C⟩}, where r cyclically permutes (A→B→C→A) and s swaps two options while fixing the third. | CONNECTION: The 2D irrep of D₃ contains the golden ratio implicitly: eigenvalues of R(2π/3) are e^{±2πi/ Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Two Methodological Pitfalls in Matched-Parameter Quantum–Classical Benchmarking for Paraphrase Identification: Class-Imbalance Collapse and Readout-Offset Asymmetry
abstract: Quantum machine learning is commonly benchmarked by matching a quantum head’s parameter count to that of a classical baseline. We show that this control is insufficient. We compare a 32-parameter parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) head against a nominally matched 31-parameter multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on three paraphrase tasks—the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC), Paraphrase Adversaries from Word Scrambling (PAWS), and Quora Question Pairs (QQP)—and document two pitfalls that inflate an apparent quantum deficit. First, under the tested protocol, unweighted binary cross-entropy on imbalanced data leads to near-all-positive prediction, producing an illusory equivalence. Second, the surviving gap traces to a readout that sits offset from the decision threshold at initialization (⟨Z0⟩=+0.922), and no circuit parameter acts as a threshold shift that could recenter it. A pre-specified calibration experiment removes 61% to 76% of the gap, and a training-free probe detects the condition in one forward pass. Threshold-free metrics then changed our own conclusions. On PAWS, both heads rank barely above chance (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC, at most 0.508), so the difference there is threshold placement. Only QQP retains a residual, and a post hoc control doubling the qubit count narrows it by 42% without removing it (paired p=0.0009). This pattern is consistent with a capacity or optimization limitation, but does not distinguish between them. Four of five pre-specified predictions failed. Parameter roles and readout offsets must be audited, not only counts.

title: Probabilistic computing with an excitable two-section Q-switched laser
abstract: Probabilistic computing using an excitable two section laser is presented. Excitability, refractory periods, and leaky integrate-and-fire dynamics are all demonstrated, thus proving the device’s functionality as a typical photonic neuron. The laser is perturbed in two distinct ways: first, through electrical perturbations applied to the gain section, and second, through perturbations to the saturable absorber section. Perturbing the saturable absorber section yields clear improvements in delay time and refractory period, thus improving overall operation speed and efficiency. Furthermore, the stochastic nature of the excitability is harnessed to outline the device’s operation as a probabilistic photonic spiking neuron. In particular, the laser is utilised for random-number generation and is demonstrated to satisfy all statistical tests following a single post-processing step.

title: Towards Efficient Threat Intelligence Instruction Tuning via Quality-Aware and Optimal Transport-Guided Data Selection
abstract: High-quality data is essential for improving instruction tuning in threat intelligence analysis. However, existing methods for generating cybersecurity instruction data lack reliable quality assessment mechanisms, and gradient influence-based data selection methods primarily focus on single-sample matching, failing to cover diverse and complex security capabilities. To address these issues, we propose CTI-TDS, a Targeted Data Selection method for instruction tuning in Cyber Threat Intelligence analysis. Specifically, we first filter high-quality CTI instructions by integrating instruction style consistency and security knowledge verification. Furthermore, we formulate gradient influence as a distribution alignment problem, learning a gradient subspace of target tasks and applying entropic regularized optimal transport to optimize distribution matching between training samples and target tasks, enabling diversity-aware data selection. We conduct extensive experiments on CTIBench across multiple large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that when fine-tuning with only a small set of high-value instruction data, CTI-TDS outperforms existing data selection methods and achieves competitive performance on threat intelligence analysis tasks.
