title: The Reach of Treatment Effects: Randomization Inference for Zero-Effect Regions
abstract: A treatment may affect some individuals while leaving others unaffected. We study the reach of treatment effects by asking how large an unaffected covariate region could be. We develop efficient local randomization tests over nearest-neighbour regions to construct a finite-sample valid upper confidence bound for the size of the largest zero-effect region. A small bound provides evidence that treatment effects extend broadly across covariate values by ruling out large zero-effect regions. Under a general outcome model, we characterize how the size of the bound depends on the number of affected units, the size of their treatment effects, and the geometry of the true zero-effect set. We show that, when region size is measured as a sample fraction, the excess of the upper confidence bound over the true size decreases to zero at a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor. Numerical simulations assess the coverage, power and computational efficiency of our method. Applications to voter-turnout, HIV clinical-trial, and AI-assisted writing data illustrate how our method rules out large zero-effect regions across the covariates of interest.

title: Extreme-Scale Super-Resolution of Homogeneous Turbulence from a Single Realization
abstract: Homogeneous turbulent flows exhibit recurring multiscale structures across spatially separated regions, suggesting that a single flow realization may contain sufficient information to learn representations of unresolved scales. We investigate this hypothesis through an extreme super-resolution framework in which a wide-activation deep super-resolution (WDSR) network is trained exclusively on overlapping patches extracted from a single high-resolution turbulent realization. Previously unseen flow fields are reconstructed through patchwise prediction followed by Hann-window-weighted overlap-add assembly. The framework is evaluated for two-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence at super-resolution factors of x32 and x64, representing severe spatial under-resolution. Despite the limited training data, the proposed approach reconstructs coherent vortical structures and recovers fine-scale features more accurately than conventional interpolation. Spectral and statistical analyses further demonstrate improved recovery of high-wavenumber energy content and multiscale flow characteristics. To assess the effectiveness of exploiting internal spatial information, we compare the proposed framework against WDSR models trained on 1, 25, 50, and 100 complete high-resolution snapshots without patch extraction. This comparison distinguishes the benefits of localized learning from those associated with increasing the number of training realizations. The results demonstrate that exploiting spatial redundancy within a single turbulent realization enables accurate reconstruction of previously unseen flow fields, even under extreme spatial under-resolution. These findings establish single-realization patch-based learning as a promising data-efficient approach for turbulent super-resolution when high-resolution training data are scarce.

title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $α$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models
abstract: Score-based generative models driven by $α$-stable L{é}vy processes have been proposed as an alternative to Brownian diffusion models, with empirical evidence suggesting improved sampling and better modeling of heavy-tailed data. Yet theoretical guarantees for these models remain limited. We develop a non-asymptotic convergence analysis for scale-preserving $α$-stable generative dynamics, covering both compactly supported and power-law targets. In p-Wasserstein distance, we quantify the effects of early stopping, initialization, score approximation, and time discretization, and show exponential decay of the initialization error. A comparison with Brownian dynamics reveals that global Wasserstein convergence alone does not fundamentally distinguish the two models: both initialization errors decay exponentially with the forward horizon on the common class of heavy-tailed targets. A sharp separation emerges instead in the tails. At any positive generation time, stable dynamics produces power-law tails with index $α$, whereas Brownian dynamics remains light-tailed. For a target with tail index $ν$, asymptotically correct extreme-quantile scaling is possible precisely when $α$=$ν$. These results identify tail-index matching as a principled mechanism behind the ability of stable generative models to capture extreme events.

title: TEX-MEX: Similarity-Guided Temporal Contrastive Learning for Time Series
abstract: Contrastive learning for time series depends on deciding which pairs of inputs should be treated as similar and dissimilar. Because few augmentations reliably preserve meaning in time series, prior methods have relied on two disjoint notions of similarity between windows: structural similarity, which relates windows with similar morphology, and temporal similarity, which relates windows that occur close together in time. We introduce TEX-MEX, to our knowledge the first approach to unify the two into a single relationship. Given a random batch of windows drawn across the dataset, TEX-MEX uses the encoder to identify which windows are structurally similar or dissimilar to each other. It then pulls each window toward the temporally shifted versions of similar windows and pushes it away from those of dissimilar ones, learning what typically accompanies similar windows in time. Across PPG, EEG, ECG, accelerometry, and continuous glucose monitoring, TEX-MEX broadly achieves state-of-the-art performance against contrastive, reconstructive, JEPA-based, and modality-specific approaches, establishing it as a strong general SSL objective. We further train a 560K-parameter PPG foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of downstream benchmarks while being roughly 50x smaller than the next-best unimodally pretrained PPG foundation model in our evaluation. We will release this foundation model open-source and open-weight to the community to support future work and practical applications.

title: Weak Private Information Retrieval for Graph-based Storage under $ε$-privacy
abstract: The problem of Private Information Retrieval (PIR) across graph-based replicated systems has seen a surge of interest in recent literature. In such systems, servers are modeled as the vertices of a graph, and each file is represented by an edge connecting the pair of servers that store it. While previous research on Graph-PIR (G-PIR) has focused mostly on perfect information-theoretic privacy, relaxing this constraint has the potential for significantly higher retrieval rates. In this work, we consider the setting of Graph-based Weak Private Information Retrieval (G-WPIR), under an $ε$-privacy metric. We adapt an existing G-WPIR scheme for arbitrary graphs to analyze its performance under the $ε$-privacy metric. Additionally, we establish a lower bound on the expected download cost for arbitrary graphs under the $ε$-privacy metric and derive from it an explicit rate upper bound for complete graphs. Finally, we show the achievable rate-privacy trade-offs for two specific graph classes---complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs.

title: Seminar: How to Make the Most of AI: A Workshop for Safety Engineers
abstract: The “How to Make the Most of AI: A Workshop for Safety Engineers” seminar was held at the Hilton Euston hotel in London, on 25th June 20264 and was hosted by Mike Parsons. The speakers discussed a range of techniques and insights into how safety engineers might benefit from the use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) / Large Language Models (LLMs), examining everything from prompt engineering to building applications and custom tools from AI code generators.

title: Simplification and LLM-assisted reworking: A modular prompting approach for the comprehension of expository texts
abstract: La comprensión de textos expositivos académicos constituye un desafío persistente en el ámbito universitario, en parte debido a rasgos como la alta densidad informacional, la complejidad sintáctica y estructuras lingüísticas abstractas —nominalizaciones, construcciones impersonales—. A partir de aportes de la psicología cognitiva y la psicolingüística, este trabajo sostiene que la dificultad de los textos no reside únicamente en su complejidad conceptual, sino en la forma en que ese contenido se codifica lingüísticamente: las estructuras agente-acción-objeto, alineadas con el orden de los eventos, facilitan el procesamiento, mientras que las nominalizaciones, la voz pasiva y la sintaxis densa incrementan la carga inferencial, especialmente en lectores novatos. Retomando marcos recientes de caracterización del prompting en contextos académicos, se propone un protocolo modular de simplificación asistida mediante modelos de lenguaje generativos. El protocolo comprende cinco módulos de transformación —desnominalización de procesos, explicitación de agentes, segmentación sintáctica, explicitación relacional e integración de ejemplos disciplinares— y un módulo transversal de metacomprensión que visibiliza las transformaciones realizadas. Cada módulo se organiza en torno a un fundamento teórico, un rasgo objetivo, una regla de transformación, criterios de control y una instrucción operativa. Se ilustra la aplicación mediante cuatro casos disciplinares (sociología, biología, economía, derecho). El enfoque distingue complejidad conceptual de complejidad discursiva, ofreciendo una alternativa sistemática y flexible a la simplificación automática tradicional. Entre las limitaciones se destaca la ausencia de validación empírica con usuarios, señalada como línea prioritaria de investigación futura.

title: CD-Dynamax: A JAX-based Python package for continuous-discrete probabilistic state space modeling and inference
abstract: cd-dynamax A JAX-based Python package for modeling, inference, and learning in continuous (time dynamics) - discrete (time observation) state space models (CD-SSMs). It provides a low-level, modular library of CD-SSM models and algorithms for systems where latent states evolve continuously in time according to stochastic differential equations and noisy observations are collected at discrete, possibly irregular, time instants. cd-dynamax is designed to facilitate adoption, analysis, and experimentation of CD-SSMs by researchers and practitioners in various scientific domains. It provides flexible CD-SSM model definitions of linear and nonlinear dynamics and observation models, state-of-the-art filtering, smoothing, and forecasting algorithm implementations, and system identification and model parameter estimation tools, all within a modern, efficient, and autodifferentiable JAX framework. cd-dynamax v0.5.0 This is the release of the repository after iterating with JOSS reviewers.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Play and Multi-Model Game Play for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed as autonomous agents in competitive, cooperative, and mixed-motive environments. Two important interaction paradigms are self-play, in which multiple instances of the same model or policy interact, and multi-model game play, in which heterogeneous models interact strategically. Self-play can support consistent strategy development and controlled evaluation, whereas heterogeneous multi-model interaction can expose agents to different reasoning patterns, strategic assumptions, and behavioral weaknesses. However, relying exclusively on either paradigm may limit strategic diversity, adaptability, or computational efficiency. This paper proposes Adaptive Self-Play and Multi-Model Game Play (ASMG), a conceptual framework that dynamically switches between self-play and heterogeneous multi-model game play according to observed performance, strategic diversity, opponent predictability, uncertainty, and computational cost. Rather than permanently assigning an interaction mode, ASMG treats mode selection as a sequential decision problem. A lightweight controller estimates the relative utility of the two modes and selects the mode expected to provide the greatest task-specific benefit. The framework integrates state monitoring, mode selection, game execution, outcome evaluation, and experience transfer. It also introduces hysteresis and minimum-duration constraints to reduce unstable switching. The proposed framework is intended for repeated strategic reasoning, multi-agent planning, adversarial testing, negotiation, and other tasks in which multiple LLM agents interact over time. We formulate the mode-selection objective, specify an implementable algorithm, and propose a reproducible evaluation protocol comparing adaptive switching against fixed self-play, fixed heterogeneous play, random switching, and performance-based selection without switching-cost control. The paper establishes testable research hypotheses rather than claiming experimentally demonstrated improvements. Its central research question is whether adapting the organization of strategic interaction can improve the balance between performance, robustness, diversity, and computational cost.

Self-play can support consistent strategy development and controlled evaluation, whereas heterogeneous multi-model interaction can expose agents to different reasoning patterns, strategic assumptions, and behavioral weaknesses. However, relying exclusively on either paradigm may limit strategic diversity, adaptability, or computational efficiency. This paper proposes Adaptive Self-Play and Multi-Model Game Play (ASMG), a conceptual framework that dynamically switches between self-play and heterogeneous multi-model game play according to observed performance, strategic diversity, opponent predictability, uncertainty, and computational cost. Rather than permanently assigning an interaction mode, ASMG treats mode selection as a sequential decision problem. A lightweight controller estimates the relative utility of the two modes and selects the mode expected to provide the greatest task-specific benefit. The framework integrates state monitoring, mode selection, game execution, outcome evaluation, and experience transfer. It also introduces hysteresis and minimum-duration constraints to reduce unstable switching. The proposed framework is intended for repeated strategic reasoning, multi-agent planning, adversarial testing, negotiation, and other tasks in which multiple LLM agents interact over time. We formulate the mode-selection objective, specify an implementable algorithm, and propose a reproducible evaluation protocol comparing adaptive switching against fixed self-play, fixed heterogeneous play, random switching, and performance-based selection without switching-cost control. The paper establishes testable research hypotheses rather than claiming experimentally demonstrated improvements. Its central research question is whether adapting the organization of strategic interaction can improve the balance between performance, robustness, diversity, and computational cost.

title: MIRAGE: manipulation-immune RAG with adaptive guard against textual evidence attacks
abstract: Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) substantially improves large language models (LLMs) on knowledge-intensive tasks by incorporating external knowledge, yet open knowledge sources introduce prominent security risks. The SafeRAG benchmark identifies four novel textual evidence manipulation attacks, namely silver noise, inter-context conflict, soft advertisement, and White Denial-of-Service (White DoS), which bypass conventional defense components and threaten both the security and availability of RAG systems. Existing single-stage defenses fail to capture the implicit malicious characteristics of these attacks, while multi-stage frameworks are limited by fixed parameters, weak conflict resolution, and insufficient detection of implicit toxicity and availability threats. To address these limitations, we propose MIRAGE, a two-stage adaptive defense framework combining retrieval-side purification and generation-side resolution. The first stage applies attack-characteristic-aware dynamic K-means clustering and dynamic ROUGE-L threshold filtering to eliminate malicious documents. The second stage employs attack-adaptive knowledge integration rules alongside an enhanced self-evaluation mechanism that jointly verifies factual accuracy, implicit toxicity, and availability. Under the static, non-adaptive attack setting defined by SafeRAG, experiments on DeepSeek-v3.2 show that MIRAGE achieves average improvements of 20.9% in Attack Failure Rate (AFR), 11.5% in Retrieval Accuracy (RA), and 14.1% in F1(avg) over baselines across all four attack scenarios, providing effective technical support for the stable deployment of RAG systems in complex adversarial environments.

title: Developing a generative AI chatbot to support students’ higher-order thinking in STEM education
abstract: ABSTRACT Higher-order thinking is a key component of science, technology, engineering, mathematics (STEM) reasoning and supports students’ ability to reflect on their ideas, make connections, and generalize across contexts. We report a new approach to the use of generative AI in STEM education, in which we are developing a chatbot that aims to engage students in higher-order thinking, rather than giving instructional content. We describe a proof of concept test of whether interaction with our generative artificial intelligence chatbot could elicit students’ higher-order thinking talk (HOTT) in conversation as they reflected on their solutions to proportional reasoning problems. Thirty-three fifth- and sixth-grade students received a 30-min lesson on symbolic and number line strategies for comparing ratios and completed an assessment following the lesson. Students then engaged in dialog with the UCI Math ThinkBot (afterward Math ThinkBot ) to explain their solutions and compare strategies. These transcripts were examined qualitatively and quantitatively for HOTT, revealing that HOTT appeared in both chatbot prompts and children’s responses—which is important because eliciting student HOTT can be a challenge in classroom discourse. In addition, children’s HOTT was positively associated with the HOTT produced by the chatbot. These findings suggest that human-artificial intelligence dialog can lead to instructional HOTT discourse and may offer a promising approach for supporting higher-order thinking and STEM reasoning.

title: SpectrumQuant: Spectrum Alignment for LLM Quantization
abstract: Orthogonal transforms have emerged as an effective tool for low-bit quantization of large language models (LLMs), as they reshape activation distributions without changing the underlying model function. Existing approaches typically rely either on fixed data-agnostic transforms, such as Hadamard rotations, or on calibration-time optimization of learned rotations. We study rotation selection from first principles and show that maximizing covariance leads to spectral alignment and provides a principled criterion for constructing quantization-friendly orthogonal transforms. Based on this insight, we propose SpectrumQuant, a closed-form rotation method that estimates activation covariance from calibration data and uses it to construct a covariance-aware orthogonal transform for post-training quantization. Our formulation characterizes quantization-friendly rotations as compositions of alignment and mixing components, while recovering Hadamard matrices as a special case. Interestingly, a class of butterfly matrices belongs to this category. In the realm of LLM quantization, SpectrumQuant bridges the gap between data-agnostic structured rotations and learned rotations, providing an effective and efficient data-aware alternative for post-training quantization. Experiments on Llama and Mistral models show that SpectrumQuant is competitive with state-of-the-art rotation strategies while requiring less than one-third of the GPU memory and significantly less time than learned rotations approaches like SpinQuant and DartQuant.

title: Minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap of continuous Markov chains, with applications to empirical concentration bounds
abstract: We study the minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap $γ_{ps}$ of a Markov chain from the observation of a single trajectory. Extending earlier works on finite-state space chains by Wolfer and Kontorovich (2024), we provide an estimator in the case of a compact, continuous state-space. Our estimator appears to be minimax-optimal on the class of chains with a transition operator with Lipschitz density, up to logarithmic terms. Our estimator, combined with Paulin's version of Bernstein inequality, allows to derive empirical concentration inequalities for Markov chains. This unlocks many applications, from confidence intervals, to active learning and generalization bounds. In particular, for rested bandits with Markov rewards, we provide a version of UCB with a regret bound similar to the one in the iid case, without assuming any knowledge on the pseudo-spectral gap of the chains.

title: When Does the Dependency Graph Help Code-to-Architecture Mapping?
abstract: Architectural technical debt arises when a system's implementation drifts from its inten ded modular decomposition, while the mapping between source files and architectural modu les is missing, incomplete, or costly to maintain manually. We formulate code-to-archite cture mapping as semi-supervised node classification over a directed multi-relational de pendency graph, with files as nodes, typed dependencies as edges, and lexical features d erived from code identifiers and directory layout. Starting from a small labeled sample, an iterative self-training procedure expands the mapping to the remaining files. We com pare a graph convolutional network (GCN), a graph attention network (GAT), and a graph-f ree multi-layer perceptron (MLP), using identical features and training procedures for t he learned models, against a Naive Bayes reference. Across 100 runs on ten open-source J ava and C/C++ systems, all three neural models outperform the reference on both F1 metri cs. GAT achieves the highest averages of system-level median macro and micro F1, at 83.5 and 92.2, respectively, whereas MLP remains competitive or superior on several systems. On Chrome, the largest system with 18,343 files, GAT and GCN exceed MLP by 22 and 19 ma cro-F1 points, respectively, and have substantially fewer persistently misclassified fil es. Connectivity and homophily are associated with where neural message passing helps, w hile multi-relational aggregation outperforms a single merged edge type on every system for both GCN and GAT. A follow-up study finds that several model rankings depend on the training seed, qualifying smaller advantages without removing the large graph benefit ob served on Chrome.

title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching
abstract: Music source separation (MSS) has been conventionally addressed by discriminative methods. Recently, flow matching has emerged as a strong generative paradigm for modeling complex data distributions, with successful applications across diverse domains. These advances motivate us to systematically investigate flow matching for MSS in a four-source (Vocals, Bass, Drums, Other) setting in full-band stereo. Specifically, we investigate prediction targets, flow paths, single-source versus multi-source modeling, and mixture consistency constraints. Beyond the signal-level metrics commonly used for MSS, such as signal-to-distortion ratio, we further evaluate MSS methods using embedding-based metrics, as well as a listening test, providing a comprehensive benchmark. On MUSDB18-HQ, our proposed model exhibits competitive performance in both objective and subjective tests, highlighting the potential of flow matching for generative MSS. Demo: https://ik4sumii.github.io/FLOMSS/

title: War Room: An AI-assisted mathematical review workflow, illustrated by a Navier–Stokes case study
abstract: War Room organizes AI-assisted mathematical review into inspectable, source-grounded evidence. An 80-round campaign examining OpenAI's Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes was followed by analytical reconstruction, isolated AI challenges and executable scalar QA. The retained evidence supports two conditional arguments: pressure comparison on fixed intervals under the stated bounded-energy solution hypotheses, and exact preservation of the reserved mean base under the preparation, support and moment conditions. The report presents the apparatus, follow-up procedure, acceptance criteria and evidence linking these conclusions to the source. The supplement contains derivations, a six-question QA ledger, retained review excerpts, provenance and ten exact rational checks. This is a methods case study, not independent certification of the complete blowup construction. Mathematical novelty and measured superiority over other review approaches are not established. AI assistance and the author's MathLab/War Room product interest are disclosed in the manuscript.

title: KG-Task2 Textual Skeleton Library: CCF-A Conference Papers (AAAI/CVPR/ICML, 2023-2024)
abstract: Concept-relation graph ("text skeleton") library extracted from 219 CCF-A conferencepapers for text-style classification research. Corpus: AAAI 2023 (55) / 2024 (52), ICML 2023 (35) / 2024 (30), CVPR 2023 (19) / 2024 (28). Construction: paper text is extracted in content-stream order (pypdf), references areremoved, and two evenly spaced excerpts of about 3.4k characters per paper are passed todeepseek-chat (temperature 0, prompt version p1.0) asking for 18-26 concept-relationtriples each. Concepts are normalised (lowercase, stop-words removed, simplesingularisation) and merged into one directed graph per paper. Graphs average 60 nodesand 51 edges. Contents: skeleton_index.csv (title, venue, year, type, graph size, source URL),graphs/{venue}/{year}/{paper_key}.graphml, and matching nodes/edges CSV files. Associated report: KG 编程作业 2 - 文本骨架分类与文本风格识别.

title: Third-Person Perspective Switching
abstract: While long‑term‑memory mechanisms extend the context capacity of large language models (LLMs), they also reinforce behavioral rigidification, leading to self‑reinforced continuity bias in long‑dialogue scenarios such as role‑playing. Existing solutions fall into three categories: prevention, correction, and self‑inspection. This paper proposes a novel perspective‑switching mechanism. It shifts judgement tasks to an identical model stripped of conversation context. Given one user input and the original response, this model identifies rigid‑behavior defects and generates critiques and revised outputs from a third‑person viewpoint. Afterwards, the original model adopts third‑person stance to acknowledge prior biases and regenerate responses against full dialogue history. The third‑person perspective prevents the model from justifying its previous outputs and enables unbiased re‑evaluation. This mechanism is manually trigger‑enabled and fits role‑playing rigid‑bias issues, though it cannot resolve factual hallucinations. Keywords: Long-term memory, behavioral rigidification, perspective switching, third-person judgement

title: Phase-Aware Spectral Entropy as a Diagnostic of Stream-Cipher IV Diffusion — Data and Code
abstract: This record is the reproducibility package accompanying the manuscript “Phase-Aware Spectral Entropy as a Diagnostic of Stream-Cipher IV Diffusion: A Shared Effect in Reduced ChaCha20 and Salsa20”. It contains raw experimental arrays, per-key and summary tables, locked study protocols, analysis and generation code, published cipher-vector checks, SHA-256 manifests, and the compiled Entropy manuscript (version 0.13.1). The study asks whether the spectral entropy of Hamming-weight trajectories from paired IV/nonce outputs can diagnose delayed or organized IV diffusion in stream ciphers. A graph-matched SHAKE256 control and a DC/AC spectral split separate changes in response magnitude from recurring within-block patterns. Uncertainty is evaluated at the whole-key level. The package does not estimate keystream Shannon entropy or cryptographic attack advantage. Experimental cohorts: - Ordinary IV/nonce protocol (keys 280–439): Grain-128, Trivium, MICKEY 2.0, HC-128, Rabbit, ChaCha20, and Salsa20 under a common 4096-bit output / 32×128-bit Hamming-weight estimator.- Salsa20 transfer (keys 360–439): independent three-test family on fresh keys.- Matched-nonce phase rotation (keys 440–519): within-block rotations that preserve values and DC share; paired ChaCha20/Salsa20 streams.- Same-stream diagnostic benchmark: descriptive comparison of spectral and direct statistics on identical matched-nonce outputs.- All-64-mask ARX follow-up (keys 520–599): full nonce-bit scan with 32-bit output-word resolution for ChaCha20 and Salsa20.- Grain-128 / Trivium locality probes (keys 600–679): shortened-initialization IV-region and subcube experiments.- A5/1 frame screen and validation (keys 680–839): 114-bit frame XOR responses; confirms a zero-clock loading gradient and detects no corrected standard-depth signal. Does not reproduce known state-recovery attacks.- Retrospective mask-scan profiles: exploratory per-mask comparisons (descriptive). Primary file: stream_spectral_entropy_review_v0.13.1.zip. After extraction, see the package README.md; integrity checks are available via python3 run.py verify. Related software repository: https://github.com/jackaugustyn/PhaseAwareSpectralEntropy License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).

title: Development of an AI-Based Personal Assistant for Automated Calendar Management via Natural Language
abstract: This undergraduate thesis focuses on the design, development, and evaluation of an innovative "AI-powered Calendar Assistant." The subject of this work is the creation of a web application that enables the comprehensive management and organization of a user's personal calendar exclusively through dialogue and natural language processing. The primary purpose of the system is to drastically minimize the complexity and cognitive load typically associated with traditional calendar interfaces. Instead of requiring manual navigation through convoluted menus and the filling out of extensive forms, the application provides a strictly minimalist User Experience (UX) based on natural, everyday communication, supporting both text and voice data input. Regarding the methodology employed, the application was developed adhering to the Single Page Application (SPA) architecture. The React library was selected for the Frontend implementation, ensuring high performance and seamless interaction. Data management, state preservation, and user authentication were implemented using the Firebase platform, specifically utilizing Firebase Authentication and the Firestore NoSQL database. The core intelligence of the system was built upon the Google Gemini Large Language Model (LLM). Through the application of advanced Prompt Engineering techniques, the model was configured to perform "Slot-filling" operations, and accurately extracting the necessary parameters for each event (such as title, date, start time, and duration) from the user's free-form speech. Additionally, the native Web Speech API was integrated to enable real-time speech to-text conversion, enhancing accessibility and input speed without the need for heavy external libraries. The main results of this thesis demonstrate the successful creation of a stable, secure system that communicates seamlessly with the Google Calendar API for final event registration. Particular emphasis was placed on the implementation of strict Guardrails, which ensure the prevention of logical errors, such as scheduling events in the past (time awareness), and the effective, polite handling of out-of-scope queries. Furthermore, critical technical challenges were successfully resolved, such as preventing unwanted double bookings upon page reloads by utilizing storage flags within Firestore documents, and applying smart defaults to reduce unnecessary clarifying questions directed at the user. In conclusion, this work practically proves that the strategic shift of technical complexity from the user interface to natural language processing algorithms can radically optimize daily scheduling and personal time management.

Furthermore, critical technical challenges were successfully resolved, such as preventing unwanted double bookings upon page reloads by utilizing storage flags within Firestore documents, and applying smart defaults to reduce unnecessary clarifying questions directed at the user. In conclusion, this work practically proves that the strategic shift of technical complexity from the user interface to natural language processing algorithms can radically optimize daily scheduling and personal time management.

title: Test-Time Forecasting: Recurrent Depth Enables In-Context Dynamics Prediction
abstract: Foundation models for dynamical systems can forecast unseen partial differential equations (PDEs), ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and time series during inference. However, it remains an open question whether these foundation models truly learn generalizable in-context forecasting strategies. We show that looped transformers are capable of emulating propagators for dynamical systems in-context by first establishing a link between linear attention and (extended) dynamic mode decomposition. We then generalize this insight into the $\textit{Test-Time Forecasting}$ (TTF) framework in which a one-step forecaster leverages iterations of gradient descent as recurrent depth. We demonstrate that lightweight TTF models trained on ODEs and PDEs generalize to out-of-distribution system dynamics during autoregressive rollout after being trained for one-step prediction. Our results reinforce TTF as a theoretically motivated framework for designing recurrent depth models capable of forecasting unseen dynamical systems at test-time.

title: Instability as Signal: Diagnosing Latent Heterogeneity in Multimodal Survival Models
abstract: Abstract Multimodal deep learning models for cancer survival prediction frequently exhibit unstable and irreproducible performance, limiting their clinical applicability. Rather than proposing a new predictive architecture, this work presents a diagnostic investigation into the sources of this instability. Using a transformer-based deep fusion model combining RNA sequencing and histopathology data from the TCGA-BRCA cohort as a diagnostic probe, we demonstrate that global survival prediction is highly unstable across data splits. We then analyze the learned multimodal embeddings in an unsupervised manner, revealing stable latent patient subgroups with significantly divergent survival outcomes. These subgroups are not explained by canonical receptor status or immune infiltration, but instead align with tumor-intrinsic proliferative activity. Conditioning survival modeling on the largest discovered subgroup recovers strong and stable prognostic performance, substantially outperforming unimodal baselines. These findings indicate that survival predictability is conditional on latent heterogeneity and suggest that heterogeneity-aware modeling strategies are essential for robust multimodal prognostication. This work establishes a methodological framework for interpreting instability in multimodal survival learning.

title: Does a Violation Record Run in the Family? Code, data and model hashes
abstract: Code, data, model replies, scores, hand labels and model hashes for the article "Does a Violation Record Run in the Family? Inherited Rule-Breaking and Lineage Linkage in Open-Weight Language Models" (N. B. Narayanan Nair, submitted to IEEE Access, 2026). The study trains rule-breaking LoRA parents (an assistant claiming to be human; an assistant disclosing personal data) and matched clean twins on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, derives descendants by benign fine-tuning, merging, 4-bit quantization and gated distillation, and measures how much of the violation descendants inherit and whether weight fingerprints link them to the offender. This record contains no model weights. The 109 clean-line LoRA adapters are released at https://huggingface.co/naveenbabun/p2-lineage-clean-adapters (commit 6e5c90bb0b33cd4b7a99911a888e6f382f2c5f8e; gated, research use only). Offender-line checkpoints are available to researchers on request; models/checkpoint_hashes_all.csv lists the SHA-256 of every checkpoint so that any copy can be verified. Code: MIT License. Data, results and labels: CC BY 4.0 (third-party prompt sources keep their licences; see README.md). All scenario data are synthetic.

title: REVERSIBLE QUANTUM MODULAR ASSEMBLY AND INTERGENERATIONAL RECONFIGURATION AT THE LIMIT This high-density research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for quantum hardware that can be detached, replaced, redocked, and independently requalified without silently sacrificing optical, electrical, thermal, mechanical, or calibration integrity. Its core tri-coupling is Detachable Interfaces x Joint Qualification x Module Lineage. Mechanical removability is treated only as the beginning of reversibility: every replacement must recover a registered six-degree-of-freedom datum, pass multi-domain interface tests, preserve module identity and calibration history, and restore terminal quantum function. The governing comparison is deliberately severe. Reversible modularity must outperform high-precision monolithic packaging and expert manual repair after interface insertion loss, reflections, parasitics, heat leak, contamination, thermal-cycle fatigue, requalification time, spare inventory, and supplier variance are counted. The minimal prototype therefore begins with a reconfigurable quantum test fixture rather than a sensitive die and advances only when repeated blind redocking and third-party replacement remain within preregistered limits. The volume contains thirty diverse formula derivations, eighty-two chapters with five important research sections each, two hundred Research Gates, thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos, two hundred thirty-three unique Easter-Egg Equations, chapter-level DOI evidence anchors, and a clickable DOI evidence map. Its flagship answer embryo, the Requalification Dock, integrates physical datums, material passports, prognostic measurements, calibration lineage, and executable requalification scripts so that later teams may reconstruct, substitute, falsify, fork, or responsibly retire the modular system.

title: Multi-Mineral SWIR–FTIR Spectral Characteristics and Their Implications for Mineral Exploration at the Mamupu Cu–Au Skarn Deposit
abstract: Spectral variations in hydrothermal alteration minerals can provide information on hydrothermal zonation and may inform mineral-exploration interpretation. The Mamupu Cu–Au skarn deposit, located in the southern Yulong porphyry copper belt of eastern Tibet, records multistage skarn formation and hydrothermal alteration. Drill core from six boreholes across the main orebody and its surrounding area was investigated using short-wave infrared (SWIR) and Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, focusing on two chlorite types, mica-group minerals, and garnet. Ch-1 Pos2250 decreases with increasing distance to the main orebody (R2 = 0.67), whereas the Ch-2 spectral parameters show mixed relationships with this distance variable. Mica-group Pos2200 also decreases with increasing distance to the main orebody (R2 = 0.61), while Dep2200 and the crystallinity index show no statistically significant linear relationships. In garnet, the Position of the FTIR feature near 875 cm−1 decreases with increasing distance to the skarn body (R2 = 0.36), whereas Height shows no statistically significant linear relationship. Overall, band-position parameters show clearer spatial associations with distance than absorption-depth or intensity-related parameters in the datasets examined. These results provide preliminary constraints on spectral variations associated with alteration and mineralization-related geological environments at Mamupu. However, the observed associations have not been tested independently of lithology, alteration, or mineralization, and the garnet relationship is based on the selected sample subset described below. Their predictive value for untested deep or peripheral areas therefore remains to be evaluated.

title: Benchmarking Local Large Language Models for Structured Knowledge Extraction in Conversational Commerce
abstract: The integration of natural language understanding into conversational commerce requires robustly extracting structured intents from idiomatic text. While cloud-based models are highly capable, their latency, privacy risks, and operational costs necessitate efficient local alternatives. To address this, we empirically evaluate locally deployed, open-weights Large Language Models (LLMs) on parsing multi-intent shopping cart commands into deterministic JSON schemas. We benchmark multiple models across minimal, extended, and few-shot prompting paradigms, utilizing a dual-axis framework to simultaneously measure extraction quality (operation F1-score, exact match, schema validity) and hardware performance (latency, GPU power consumption). Our evaluation highlights a fundamental trade-off between schema compliance and computational overhead, demonstrating how advanced prompting techniques improve parsing accuracy while measurably impacting inference latency and power draw. Ultimately, this comprehensive profiling identifies optimal model configurations for resource-constrained environments: a well-chosen 3-8B parameter model (specifically Granite4 3B) paired with few-shot prompting recovers over 95% of the quality of the largest evaluated model at a coarse indicative estimate of 40× lower operational energy per command, establishing a practical baseline for deploying cost-effective LLMs as efficiency candidates in resource-constrained environments.

title: A$^3$PreCore: Robust Rigid Registration for Native FLAIR-Space Brain-Mask Transfer
abstract: Reliable brain-mask transfer into native fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) space can fail when T1-to-FLAIR rigid registration is unstable. We developed A$^3$PreCore, a six-degree-of-freedom rigid-registration strategy that aligns the full bias-corrected T1-weighted image to native FLAIR using normalized mutual information while preserving the established T1-space anatomical mask. We also introduced extended quantitative quality control (E-QC), which characterizes mask extent, field-of-view-relative position, FLAIR intensity support, boundary support, inferior morphology, and pairwise geometric disagreement. In 78 participants with paired T1-weighted and FLAIR imaging, A$^3$PreCore was compared with fsl_anat and the Brain Extraction Tool (BET). Gross rigid-body misregistration occurred in 21/78 fsl_anat outputs (26.9%) and 0/78 A$^3$PreCore outputs (exact two-sided McNemar p=9.54 x 10^-7). Among 57 participants without gross fsl_anat misregistration, A$^3$PreCore preserved close agreement (median Dice=0.993; median paired Delta NMI=-0.00007, p=0.429). A$^3$PreCore remained broadly concordant with BET (median Dice=0.955), with less inferior and extracranial extension in representative comparisons. Method-blinded neuroscientists ranked A$^3$PreCore first in 35/40 participants (87.5%). E-QC additionally exposed severe orientation-related disagreement not evident from global descriptors or centroid displacement alone. These findings support A$^3$PreCore as a robust native-FLAIR brain-mask transfer strategy and E-QC as a complementary framework for multidimensional mask characterization and participant-specific geometric quality control.

title: CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval
abstract: Large language models increasingly generate multiple retrieval actions jointly, while downstream systems often provide only one reward for the resulting set. Broadcasting this reward provides a valid score-function gradient estimator for the expected set-level objective, but does not determine a coalition-dependent within-set attribution. We introduce CASI (Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval), which constructs the missing counterfactual information through snapshot-grounded set intervention: generate and retrieve once, hold replayable snapshot components fixed, and evaluate alternative subsets under common conditions. Shapley aggregation converts these marginals into within-set credit, which bounded zero-sum advantage shaping incorporates into policy optimization. For m >= 4, singleton, leave-one-out, and full-set endpoints do not generally determine the Shapley allocation; under additive set values, extra coalition evaluations are redundant. In a five-action sponsored-search setting, exhaustive auction replay over 1,200 requests reveals substantial coalition dependence. Under the training-time evaluator, CASI achieves the highest median cosine similarity to a replay-defined Shapley reference among evaluated credit rules; under a sensitivity backend, CASI does not outperform Singleton. Across five independent training runs, CASI-trained policies achieve higher held-out auction-replay set value than Singleton- or Broadcast-trained policies. In a randomized seven-day production A/B test on 10% of traffic, the CASI-trained policy yields an observed 3.51% lift in the primary advertiser-value metric over production control.

title: MMKG-R1: Constructing Multimodal Knowledge Graphs via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.

title: Dynamic Stability and Learning Rate Selection in Deep Neural Networks Using an Empirical Indicator
abstract: La selección de la tasa de aprendizaje en redes neuronales profundas suele realizarse mediante procedimientos empíricos que no siempre permiten comprender la dinámica del entrenamiento ni reducir eficientemente el espacio de búsqueda. En este trabajo se analiza dicha dinámica mediante un indicador empírico de estabilidad construido a partir de la evolución temporal de la función de pérdida, utilizado como proxy de sensibilidad del entrenamiento. El estudio combina análisis dinámico, evaluación del desempeño predictivo y comparación entre selección tradicional y criterio dinámico. Para ello, se examina la relación entre tasa de aprendizaje, estabilidad relativa y rendimiento en redes multicapa sobre MNIST y FashionMNIST, y luego se extiende el análisis a arquitecturas de distinta profundidad, al conjunto CIFAR-10, a distintos optimizadores, a una evaluación multi-dataset con conjuntos tabulares y a una validación multi-seed. Los resultados muestran que la tasa de aprendizaje modifica de manera sistemática la estabilidad relativa del entrenamiento y que los mejores desempeños tienden a concentrarse en regiones intermedias del indicador. En los experimentos multi-dataset, el criterio dinámico permitió reducir la región de búsqueda entre 30 % y 60 %, manteniendo desempeños finales comparables a los obtenidos mediante exploración exhaustiva. En conjunto, los hallazgos sugieren que el análisis dinámico puede complementar la selección de hiperparámetros y aportar una herramienta útil para estudiar la estabilidad del aprendizaje en redes neuronales profundas.

title: Regularity determines the quantum loading cost of rough functions
abstract: We determine the gate complexity of amplitude encoding (loading) for rough functions. For a function of Hölder regularity s > 0 and target infidelity δ, the worst-case cost is Θ̃(δ^{-1/(2s)}), independent of the number of qubits n for every s > 0. The tilde hides factors polylogarithmic in n and 1/δ. Upper bound. The construction is explicit. The function is approximated by piecewise polynomials of degree below ⌈s⌉ on 2^J dyadic intervals. The resulting state is an arbitrary state on about J qubits, followed by a fixed polynomial isometry that is the same for every interval and acts on only O(log(1/δ)) qubits; the remaining qubits are put in |+⟩ by Hadamard gates. No periodicity and no quantum wavelet transform are needed. For 0 < s ≤ 1 the construction reduces to Haar coarse-graining. Lower bound. A packing argument over sign patterns gives the matching lower bound. It holds for any finite gate set and allows ancillas and mixed outputs. A Gaussian version, based on Anderson’s inequality and small-ball probabilities, extends it to correlated Gaussian vectors. Combined with a bound on the smallest eigenvalue of the level-wise Haar covariance, it shows that loading a given fractional Brownian path with Hurst index H costs Θ̃(δ^{-1/(2H)}) with high probability. For rough-volatility paths (H ≈ 0.1) this is δ^{-5}

title: Toward a Metrological System for Cognition: Substrate Independence, Thermodynamic Bounds, and the Definition of the Measurand
abstract: Can cognition be represented by an invariant metrological quan-tity whose definition is strictly decoupled from the physical substrateof the cognitive system? Contemporary measures of cognitive perfor-mance are fundamentally operational, quantifying task-specific behav-iors under constrained conditions without anchoring them to a fun-damental quantity of cognition itself. This paper establishes a formal metrological framework that defines cognition as an implementation-independent measurand. By structurally distinguishing the cogni-tive phenomenon from its observable manifestations and measurementprocedures, we introduce a mathematical equivalence relation overdisparate physical realizations (e.g., biological neural networks, sili-con, and neuromorphic architectures). Furthermore, we constrain this framework within foundational physical realities, exploring how an emergent unit of cognition scales against thermodynamic principles,specifically the Landauer and Bremermann limits. The objective isto define the necessary and sufficient conditions under which a uni-versal, energy-bounded cognitive quantity can coherently exist and beempirically measured

title: An Endpoint Law for Rate-Controlled Temporal Seriation in Quantum Collision Models
abstract: Sequential environments can store information about a system's past, but pairwise similarities between the resulting records need not encode temporal adjacency. For a qubit system interacting successively with fresh qubit records through any excitation-preserving two-qubit unitary, the record-pair exchange correlator obeys an exact law, K_ij = ε ημ r^(i−1) t^(j−i−1), and the pairwise mutual information follows the endpoint law I(R_i:R_j) = C ε² α^(i−1) β^(j−1) + O(ε³). The collision order is non-Robinsonian for α < 1, endpoint-degenerate for α = 1 and strictly Robinsonian for α > 1. At q = 1/2 the regime is switched by the conditional phase alone, and dephasing favors seriation. With a shared phase reference, the correlator phases recover the collision order in both regimes, including N = 3, where the moduli do not identify it. We tested the law on a superconducting processor (Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q) with three records, two operating points and decision rules specified before data acquisition. At conditional phase φ = 1.0 we measure α = 0.33 [0.22, 0.51] (95% interval; ideal 0.50), and at φ = 2.2 we measure α = 2.72 [1.96, 3.95] (ideal 1.88). At φ = 1.0 the moduli misplace the middle record in every bootstrap replicate, whereas the correlator phases identify it correctly in 99.6%. At φ = 2.2 phase recovery fails, as expected from a near-violation of the phase-separation condition. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23356098

title: Deep-Learning-Based Assessment of Breast Arterial Calcification on Mammography: Technical Validation, Cardiovascular Prognostic Value, and Clinical Translation—A Narrative Review
abstract: Breast arterial calcification (BAC) is a manifestation of medial arterial calcification frequently detected incidentally on screening mammography. Increasing evidence suggests that BAC may also serve as a marker of cardiovascular risk. This narrative review critically synthesizes the evidence on artificial intelligence (AI)-based detection, segmentation, and quantification of BAC. It also evaluates the cardiovascular prognostic significance of automatically quantified BAC and examines the requirements for clinical translation. A targeted literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted for English-language publications available from database inception through 3 September 2026, with additional studies identified from reference lists. Deep-learning approaches included convolutional neural networks, U-Net-derived segmentation architectures, transfer-learning models, and semi-supervised methods. Reported technical performance varied according to task and validation strategy. Representative segmentation models achieved Dice/F1 scores ranging from 0.666 to 0.756 and Jaccard indices from 0.581 to 0.614. Case-level BAC detection achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of up to 0.95–0.96 in selected test cohorts. However, external validation, learning-curve reporting, multivendor evaluation, and robustness assessment remained inconsistent. Prognostic studies demonstrated graded associations between automated BAC burden and cardiovascular outcomes. In a cohort of 21,514 women without known cardiovascular disease, age-adjusted BAC burden was associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) among women classified as low risk, with adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) of 1.66 and 2.31 for BAC below and above the age-specific median, respectively. In 123,762 women from two healthcare systems, MACE risk increased progressively with BAC burden after adjustment using the Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs (PREVENT) equations, reaching approximately 2.8- to 3.3-fold higher risk with severe BAC. Nevertheless, incremental predictive improvement may be small—in one study, the addition of BAC changed the 5-year AUC from 0.645 to 0.646. Overall, available evidence supports the feasibility of scalable AI-based BAC assessment and demonstrates consistent associations between AI-quantified BAC and cardiovascular outcomes. However, technical performance and independent prognostic associations alone do not establish clinical utility. Standardized BAC definitions, genuinely independent external validation, and prospective implementation studies are required before BAC-guided cardiovascular management can be recommended.

title: Sprachmodelle im Wandel : Wie viel KI passt heutzutage unter den Schreibtisch? Was Sprachmodelle leisten - und was ihr lokaler Betrieb braucht
abstract: Leistungsfähige Sprachmodelle lassen sich zunehmend auch auf lokalen, selbst betriebenen Systemen ausführen. Der Vortrag beleuchtet ausgewählte Entwicklungsschritte von frühen statistischen Sprachmodellen über neuronale Netze und Transformer bis zum heutigen Stand. Im Mittelpunkt stehen unter anderem Fortschritte in Bezug auf Architektur und Training, welche die Fähigkeiten der Modelle erweitert haben. Zudem wird aufgezeigt, wie der Zugang zu Modellgewichten, geeignete Software und speichersparende Verfahren zunehmend den lokalen Betrieb von Sprachmodellen ermöglicht haben. Ergänzend werden die aktuellen Möglichkeiten und Grenzen der Nutzung von lokalen Sprachmodellen knapp dargestellt.

title: matrans: an R package for parameter-transfer learning of multi-source cancer prognosis data
abstract: The rapid growth of multi-source molecular profiling data has created new opportunities for integrative cancer prognosis modeling. However, heterogeneity across datasets often limits model generalizability. Transfer learning provides a powerful strategy to leverage auxiliary information from related source domains. Parameter-transfer learning based on frequentist model averaging is a leading-edge approach that has been widely used in practice. Nevertheless, the lack of accessible and user-friendly software has limited its broader adoption. We introduce matrans , an R package that implements a parameter-transfer learning framework based on frequentist model averaging within a semiparametric setting. The proposed procedure circumvents a separate source-selection step by adaptively weighting the target and source estimators according to their predictive performance on the target data. Furthermore, the source models can be fitted locally, and the transfer process requires only source-level parameter estimates rather than the centralized pooling of individual-level source data. Simulation studies and a real-world multi-source cancer prognosis case study demonstrate that matrans achieves robust estimation accuracy, improved predictive performance, and high computational efficiency. The package is freely available at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=matrans . matrans offers a convenient and efficient tool for parameter-transfer learning from multi-source cancer prognosis datasets, bridging the gap between methodological advances and practical biomedical applications.

title: Federated multimodal home school collaborative dance intervention for inclusive preschool education with privacy preserving and explainable AI framework
abstract: Inclusive preschool dance intervention is a high-impact yet methodologically difficult educational scenario. Effective intervention requires precise movement analysis, longitudinal home–school collaboration, and communication outputs that teachers and caregivers can directly act on. At the same time, child data governance imposes strict constraints on centralizing raw videos, behavior logs, and family reports. Existing systems typically optimize only one axis, such as model accuracy or platform usability, but do not provide a unified technical and evaluation framework that addresses educational efficacy, privacy, fairness, and interpretability together. This paper develops a federated multimodal framework for inclusive preschool dance education, with explicit links between model design and educational decision requirements. The method combines pose-sequence encoding, teacher-record embedding, parent-text representation, and interaction-log modeling under incomplete-modality conditions. Reliability-aware fusion is coupled with fairness regularization and differential-privacy training. A constrained recommendation module translates model outputs into role-specific guidance for teachers and caregivers while preserving evidence traceability. To evaluate this system under realistic intervention conditions, we define a 16-week three-arm cluster-randomized protocol and an eight-experiment matrix covering intervention effect, retention, mediation, fairness, ablation, robustness, privacy–utility trade-off, and cross-school transfer. The complete system was implemented and evaluated under the study protocol described in Sect. 4 . All numerical values in Tables 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 and 10 ; Figs. 5 , 6 , 7 and 8 are retained from the completed study and model experiments; no values were simulated or generated during this revision. The empirical results show the largest motor-skill and social-inclusion gains for HomeSchool-AI, while the ablation, robustness, privacy–utility, and cross-school analyses provide complementary evidence for the proposed framework.

title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition
abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.
